subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ALLEGED LOW FLYING OF R.C.A.F. PLANES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) has asked about low flying over the cities of Winnipeg and St. James, and a report has now been received.
Since the construction of Stevenson field the city of Winnipeg has greatly expanded. Residential areas on the west side are now in danger of surrounding the airport. At the same time the international, itinerant and local civil traffic, which accounts for more than half of the total flying at this field, has increased greatly.
In order that this volume of traffic may be accommodated safely, an arrival procedure known as a circuit is sometimes necessary. This pattern which, at Winnipeg, is under the control of experienced Department of Transport officials, is done in excess of 1,000 feet above ground and permits an orderly transition to final approach. In conformance with these requirements, a number of aircraft may fly over certain areas. Residents estimating the altitude by sound alone may believe the aircraft to be low flying; whereas in fact they are at the maximum safe legal altitude for the procedure involved.
R.C.A.F. operations at Winnipeg are comprised mainly of navigator and radio officer training. This training, of course, includes night as well as day exercises. For these flights as for all other operations based at Stevenson field, only competent and qualified pilots are used.
There has not been any confirmed instance of actual low flying reported over Winnipeg with the exception of one isolated case involving an aircraft from another base. In this case, the pilot was subjected to severe disciplinary action.

47.	Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration, $502,137.

Mr. Chairman, on three or four occasions this session I have talked about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, therefore it would be a matter of repeating myself if I started to go into details. However, I had hoped that the minister would have brought in some amendments to the P.F.A.A.; in fact, I am disappointed that he did not bring in an amendment to deal with the farmer who bought land from the provincial government after 1940 and cannot participate or even get any assistance from the P.F.A.A. fund.
The fund is in this position: A man who bought crown land contributed to the fund every load of grain he sold to the elevator. That is quite definite and plain and he cannot participate in any of the benefits of the act. For that reason I do not think the government should collect from these people.
Perhaps a test case should be made of this to see if it is really possible to collect money from them without giving them any benefits. It may be wise to have a decision of the Department of Justice on this question.
I do not need to point out to the minister that this is a very sore point in the north of my constituency. I had hoped that the minister would have brought in an amendment to correct this grievance. In fact, even at this late date I ask the minister to give it some consideration.
I could never understand how the government can collect money from farmers contributing to the P.F.A.A. fund when the act distinctly says they cannot participate in the benefits.
I have had a great deal of correspondence with the minister concerning P.F.A.A. and while he was good enough to send some of

Supply-Agriculture
his officers to explain the act I am still receiving complaints from people who are wondering why they were left out.
One matter has always puzzled me and it is not because I have not endeavoured to understand it. I am referring to where the line is drawn dividing the people who can get paid on crown land and those on the south side of the line who cannot get paid.
I am going to send over to the minister a map of Selkirk constituency and I will ask him if he would be kind enough to have the officers of his department draw the line on the map so that in the future when I am challenged about it will be able to take out this map and show people where the line is.
I am not going to say any more at this time. I have conveyed to the minister the wishes of the farmers of my constituency regarding this act. The act has been of considerable value to many people in my constituency who suffered the loss of their crops. I know that the minister could improve this bill a great deal if he were to bring in amendments.
I am now sending over to the minister the map I have referred to. I hope the minister will put the line on it. If he does he will save me a lot of arguments this fall.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, while the map is being sent over I would just like to say that any change in the line would have to be made by legislation. The line has been set by legislation and I think on two different occasions the question has been raised in the house. I would say that the map which is submitted will be considered. There is some question, of course, as to where the line should be drawn across the north. It may possibly be that the line is not in exactly the right place but we will consider that before the next session and if legislation is necessary we will bring it down.
But will you be kind enough to have an officer of your department draw the line that you are dealing with now on the map I am sending over?
Oh well, that should be a simple matter for them to do and I will see that it is done.
Thank you; I hope it is done.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister a few questions regarding the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I am referring particularly to the form which farmers are forced to fill out in respect to individual farms. My first

question is this. Are the farmers left with a duplicate copy of the statements they give to the inspector?
I am sorry but I am not able to hear the question.

Are the
individual farmers left with a duplicate copy of the statement they give to the P.F.A.A. inspector when he calls around?
I understand that that has not been done in the past but it has been arranged that it will be done in the future. Someone asked that question earlier in the session.

Are all
farmers required to make a statutory declaration that the answers given to the questions asked are true?
Yes; there is to all intents and purposes a statutory declaration taken.
I understand that that will be uniform throughout the west.
That is correct.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group contend that the present payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are too low. The act was brought in in 1939 at which time a maximum payment of $2.50 per acre was provided on half the cultivated acreage up to a maximum of 400 acres. The maximum payment has been $500; when the crop yield was from 4 to 8 bushels per acre the payment has been $300.
Since 1939 the cost of production and the cost of living have eaten away most of the value of the payments that were established in 1939. Today we have a dollar which is perhaps a 50 cent or a 40 cent dollar, but still the payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act remain the same. I suggest that the time has come when the government at least should double the payments under this act. Last year the hon. member for The Battlefords brought in a resolution on behalf of this group to that effect.
I would point out that today $1,000 will buy less than $500 would have bought in 1939. There is not only that factor to be considered, there is the factor of the one per cent charge which today brings in two and a half times as much revenue as it did in 1939 because of the increase in the price of wheat. I should like to ask the minister whether any consideration has been given by his department to increasing the benefits under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, to doubling the benefits as I have suggested to the point where

a farmer would have the protection that he should receive under the act.

Mr. Chairman, as hon. members who were here throughout the sitting last night know, I dealt with this question at that time. I regret very much if my hon. friend was able to watch a football game while I remained here to take up this matter, but in any event the matter was dealt with. Just to answer the question which has been asked, I would say that we have given consideration to the matter and have decided that the act as it is at the present time does meet the situation in spite of the fact that there has been a lowering in the value of the dollar. That was provided for when the terms of the act were drawn to make it possible for a person who is affected drawing, not only the sum provided in the act but also to have earnings from the marketing of whatever grain he has. It was estimated that the increase in the price of grain or the decrease in the price would take care of any difference that occurred. Our examination of the records indicates that that has been the case. The amount which the farmer receives now, with the exception of the man who has no wheat per acre, and there are very few of those, there is anywhere from two to three bushels an acre to be sold, and when those facts are taken into consideration the return in proportion to costs is just about the same now, or a little higher in most cases, than it was in 1939.
I am sure that no one understands the gobbledegook we have just listened to now.
That is the football game you are talking about.
Any farmer knows that $500 today will not purchase as much as it did in 1939.
If my hon. friend will read my speech in reply last session he will find it is all there and it has been proven outright.
I have read it, and it is gobbledegook, but there was more gobbledegook last time than there is now because the minister took longer to say the same thing.
We get all the gobbledegook when you are speaking.

I want to tell the minister that the farmers in western Canada are completely dissatisfied with the amount paid under the act. There have been certain improvements made in the past in regard 67509-4451
Supply-Agriculture
to the area where it is paid, and that is all to the good, but the schedule of payments is completely inadequate.
I wish to say that I was in the chamber last night when the minister made his remarks on this subject, and I am sure I would have had a much more enjoyable time if I had been able to go to the football game. Last night, if I remember correctly, the minister's excuse was that there is sufficient money to pay the grocery bill. Was that not it? Today he has gone to a certain quantity of the wheat that a farmer may or may not have to be considered to have a crop failure.
You will find that is what I said last night; you were not listening.

I wish to point out that, even though the price of wheat has increased substantially since 1939, the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat is no greater today than it was in 1939, so that any wheat a farmer may have when he is said to have a crop failure, one, two or three bushels of wheat per acre will buy no more than the wheat in 1939, and the prairie farm assistance benefit is worth not much more than one-third of what it was worth in 1939.

Last year when the minister's estimates came up, I pointed out to him that there was a large area of land in western Alberta, a good part of which is in my riding, that had been exempted from the act when it was drawn up; that since that time the new methods of farming, different types of crops, new knowledge and so on have made at least part of that land productive; and that still most people, although they are paying into the P.F.A.A. all the time, are unable to get any benefits out of it. I asked the minister last year if he would consider putting that land under the act because it is now a productive area and these people are unable to come in under the benefits. I would ask the minister whether any consideration has been given to that area and, if so, what decisions were made.

As I understand it, it is the same question that was raised by the hon. member for Selkirk with regard to a section of Manitoba. That is, we amended the act some few years ago to make it impossible for lands which the government disposed of after a certain date, January 1940, to come under the act, the understanding being that should the provincial governments of Manitoba, Alberta or Saskatchewan make agreements with the farmers,-in Saskatchewan it is an agreement on a 33-year lease, and in the other two provinces it might be

Supply-Agriculture
-a sale of the land to the farmer-we maintained that if the governments in the prairie provinces were disposing of land to farmers after the date when this act came into effect they should do so on terms which made it possible for the farmer to carry on without the benefits of this act. So a line was drawn which left out from under the act the area where the lands had not yet been disposed >of or had been disposed of after that date.
Through the southern parts of the province the same thing applies, namely that where submarginal lands, as they were referred to last night, are defined as submarginal lands by the provincial governments, they do not come under this act at all. If the provincial governments' enactment adds to those lands, then those lands are taken out. We simply stated in the act at that time that if the provincial government were leasing those lands to farmers who were on adjacent lands and bringing them back under cultivation or back where they would otherwise come under the terms of this act, these lands are not covered by this act.
On the question of paying in, everybody in Canada pays in to this act. This is not an insurance bill, as was suggested a few moments ago. It is not an insurance bill in any sense of the term. If it were, we could not pass it. Insurance bills can only be passed by the provincial governments. The first thing we had to satisfy the authorities here on, including the justice department, at the time we put the act through was that this is not insurance. It is not the paying of a fee in order to get a service. When the act was first drafted, it did not have in it any terms for the paying of one per cent. After the discussions which took place in this house, the farm organizations in the west suggested that in order that it might not be said that they were getting payment from a fund which was created entirely by setting up a tax collected from all the people of Canada, they should make a special contribution, and that special contribution is in the nature of one per cent on the grain sold. Hence the one per cent is simply a payment in order to make it possible for the farmers to contribute something throughout the years towards the fact that they may collect. I would point out to my hon. friend also what happens in spite of the fact that some people who may collect may not have any grain at all. Some of the people who collect may have only livestock, and when they do have those for sale nothing is paid when they sell. If they have only livestock, they may grow some grain ih order to feed the livestock. But they collect just the same as do the people who have only wheat. Such a person does not pay

anything in, but he collects. Both sides of the picture do turn up in this particular legislation.

I understand that, Mr. Chairman; but what I wanted to know was this. What possibility is there of these people getting in? I refer to those people on what was at that time considered to be submarginal land and left out of the act until examination had been made, as a result of agreement between the provincial and federal governments. I was wondering what the possibility is of some of these people, on what was considered at that time as being submarginal land, getting in under the act now. Owing to improved methods and improved knowledge they are now able to grow fairly substantial crops in this area. Would it be a provincial responsibility to request that these lands be included under the act or would it be a federal responsibility or would it be a matter of negotiation between the two governments? If so, which government should initiate the discussions? Is there any possibility at all of their getting in?

My understanding is that at the time this matter was before the agriculture committee when the legislation was last going through the house, the lands in the special areas-which I presume are the lands which are referred to-in Alberta were specially dealt with in the legislation. If there is any reason for taking another look at it, we can do it along with the province. The representatives of the provincial government were here and they appeared here before the committee at the time we dealt with the matter previously. I will have to check back and see what lands are involved and if it would be necessary to have further hearings on the matter. I do not know whether or not the hon. member for Peace River recalls the discussions that took place at that time. I think he does so because his northern area was concerned. We did try to meet conditions there then. If developments have taken place which indicate that we have not met them, that matter can be discussed again.
This does not apply to the special areas. It applies to the grey wooded soil along the foot of the foothills.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. There is one question that I should like to ask the minister, but before I do so I should like to say this about the act. In the main there is satisfaction with the changes that were made some years ago and which have just been referred to in the interchange between the minister and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. Up in my country I think that those changes

were accepted with considerable enthusiasm and that they have worked well. But there is still a good deal of dissatisfaction amongst the people over two rather specific things. One is the very close definition of "farmer". The matter was dealt with last night by the minister and I can understand the position that he takes. But oftentimes people get the feeling that the regulations are used in order to cut out as many farmers as possible from receiving benefit. I am not saying that is the case, but I say that the feeling is there.
For example, here is the case of a chap who works only part time on the railroad and who works a farm close by. He operates that farm as an efficient farmer and is doing well with it. In a normal year he gets more out of his farm than he gets out of his job on the railroad. But just the same, when a year comes along when he does not get a good crop and when he applies for prairie farm assistance because the yield has fallen below 4 bushels an acre, they say this to him: "You cannot have it because your chief income this year comes from your job on the railroad." I can understand that that chap would have a case for justifiable complaint.
Justifiable homicide.

That sort of thing, I believe, is resorted to in many cases. I wonder whether it would not be possible to recast the definition of "farmer", taking into account the sort of thing I have mentioned. In these cases the people are farmers in the full sense of the word. They are carrying on quite efficiently. They feel themselves to be entitled to the benefits because they are paying what they consider to be a sort of premium.
That brings me to another point. I wonder whether the minister and his department have given consideration to what has been urged, very largely by the hon. member for Acadia, namely, that a crop insurance program be considered, and that part of what is now being done under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act be transferred to such a crop insurance program. I think the only way in which we shall ever get satisfaction out of the paying of a premium out of the product produced by the farmer will be through a crop insurance plan rather than through this prairie farm assistance. A great many of the farmers have come to look upon P.F.A.A. as a sort of crop insurance program. Whether that view is realistic or justified, they look upon it as such because they pay a premium as they think. One per cent over the years out of their production justifies them to a degree in thinking that they should receive benefits whenever their yield falls below 4 bushels an acre, whether or not they are considered to be farmers under the act.
Supply-Agriculture
Another question is this one of river lots. I wonder whether the minister has had any experience with them. As I understand it, under the act or the regulations-I cannot tell which-the river lots that are registered as river lots are treated as separate townships. Very often in the bends of these large rivers, like the Peace river, you can find areas that are called river lots and are registered in the land titles office as such.
I have not been able to find out why the department looks upon these river lots as separate townships rather than having them registered as part of the township to whichi they belong. This past year quite a number of the people who occupy river lots found themselves unable to get benefits under the act, although their own yield fell away below the eight bushels per acre. They were told by the officials in Edmonton that they could not get benefits because their river lots were registered or were looked upon by the department as separate townships, and since they were separate townships they could not be dealt with in the ordinary way.
I just wondered if the minister had much experience with that sort of thing, and if he would have an answer as to why river lots are looked upon, no matter how large or small they may be, as separate townships. Why could they not be attached, let us say, to a contiguous township for the purpose of payment under the act?

If I understand what the hon. member for Peace River has been saying with regard to the river lots it does not exactly conform to what our experience with the matter is. We did find, for the orderly administration of the act, it was impossible to bring river lots under the terms of the act. We, therefore, had a meeting with the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta where these river lots are and had an understanding reached as to what would come under the terms of this act as constituting a township. I would be surprised if any small area had been called a township, any small holding of an individual. The objective was to put enough of these river lots into an area to make up an area approximately the same as a township, and then to decide whether or not they were entitled to payment on the same basis as other townships are. It was simply a matter of defining them. There is quite a long list of them here. There are 6i pages for Manitoba, about a page for Saskatchewan and about two pages for Alberta, listing the areas that are defined.
For example, group 70 is river lot township "B", improvement district No. 102; lots 1 to 41 inclusive in township 67, range 14, west of the fourth; townships 67 and 68, range 15,

the minister to do anything about it immediately because he has already indicated that it is not the intention to bring in any amendments during the course of this session but I think it should be on the record because there are one or two excellent suggestions contained in it. The resolution reads:
Be it resolved that we petition the government of Canada for the following amendments to said act-
That is the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
(a)	Payments on crop losses to be made on the individual basis.
(b)	Payments to be based on the actual cultivated acreage in the year of the crop loss.
(c)	Payments to be made on damage from all or any natural causes.
(d)	Payments to be made to all who contribute to the scheme, or-those not eligible for payment within a qualifying area to be exempt from contributing to the plan upon application for such exemption.
(e)	A statement to be attached to payment cheque, stating upon what basis payment is being made.
In the interests of saving time I will not comment on all of these points but I do want to point out that paragraph (e) in particular is, I think, a perfectly reasonable request and would as a matter of fact save a great deal of trouble and correspondence so far as the administration is concerned.
Quite often when farmers receive their prairie farm assistance payment a cheque is sent to the farmer stating the amount and sometimes he is not able to calculate on what basis the amount was arrived at. In order to do so he has to write to the prairie farm assistance board or if it is more convenient he complains to his member of parliament who has to handle it for him. This requires correspondence back and forth, file keeping and extra unnecessary work. I think it would be quite simple to include with the cheque a statement showing on what acreage and on which parcel of land the payment is being made, the amount per acre, and the total amount. I think that would save the department a great deal of administrative work.
I might point out, too, that the situation referred to in paragraph (d)-and I do not need to enlarge upon it because it has already been discussed-is a real injustice that might be rectified. Under certain provisions of the act there are certain parcels of land which are not eligible for prairie farm assistance and particularly that land which was purchased by a farmer after January 1, 1940 from the provincial government.
Of course, that does not apply to V.L.A. land and certain other lands. There is a great deal of the kind of land I have referred to being farmed in the province of Manitoba. Farmers who farm that land and grow grain

year after year have been contributing the 1 per cent levy under the provisions of the act with no hope whatever, unless the act is eventually changed, of ever benefiting at all from the fund.
Over a period of years the 1 per cent contribution amounts to a considerable sum of money. If the government is going to take the stand that this land is sub-marginal, or for one reason or another is never to be eligible for prairie farm assistance, I think the fair thing to do would be to exclude those farmers from the 1 per cent levy.
I think there is a great element of unfairness in asking a farmer to contribute year after year 1 per cent of the value of his grain into a fund and then telling him that under no circumstances can he receive any benefit from that fund. Instead of doing it that way, I think it would be wiser either to include as much as possible of that land by entering into a new agreement with the provinces with regard to that kind of land, or else, in areas where the governments both provincial and federal feel there is no possibility of including the land, if it is definitely submarginal in their opinion, then it should be excluded from the 1 per cent levy in order to bring about some, sort of rough justice at least.

I should like to say just a few words on this item. For a number of years this group has urged the extension of the operation of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to all agricultural areas in Canada, and quite recently the hon. member for Dauphin had a private members' motion on the order paper to that effect, which received the support of all members of this party. As a British Columbia member, ever since I have been in this house I have been urging the extension of the operation of this act in the province of British Columbia, but so far none of us have been able to influence the minister or the administration in that respect.
I am just going to read a paragraph from an editorial in Country Life of September 1955, which asks the minister a question. I might mention that Country Life is the official organ of at least 98 per cent of the agricultural organizations of British Columbia and, I should think, almost a similar percentage of the farmers in the country. This is entitled "No Wonder There's No P.F.R.A. in B.C.":
From Vanderhoof came a press release this summer which indicates that the Canada and British Columbia agricultural departments are cooperating to make a survey of central British Columbia to determine the possibilities from an agricultural standpoint.
Country Life is mighty pleased to hear of this action because we feel it is long overdue.
At that, it isn't nearly enough. The work should be extended over the entire province and co-related with the future prospects of industrial development and population increase.
For years farmer groups have been hounding the province and Ottawa to have the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act enlarged to include this Pacific coast province. The appeals fall on deaf ears.
With the exception of Pemberton and VLA projects the assistance of P.F.R.A. has been denied B.C. and we cannot find it in our hearts to blame Ottawa overmuch for this oversight.
Most of the blame can be laid on the doorstep of the British Columbia government. It is little use to cry to Ottawa that B.C. needs development of its agricultural resources when no surveys have been made to provide an overall picture of the future possibilities of this graet province agriculture-wise.
We are told in a broad sweeping way that five per cent of the land in B.C. is useful for agricultural purposes. But what we haven't been told is what each untilled section can best be used for and whether there is a sound economic future in developing any particular section for agriculture.
In view of our repeated requests throughout the years for the extension of the operation of the act to British Columbia, I want to ask the minister this question. Is there some substance in the contention in this editorial, and are we wasting our breath in this house until the government of British Columbia organizes surveys of the areas suitable to the operation of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act?

The question that is raised is not just along the line that has been suggested by the editorial. I spoke to the organization for which, I think, this newspaper speaks, last fall when I was out in British Columbia, and they raised the same question as to why we did not apply P.F.R.A. to British Columbia. I indicated to them that the name itself suggested why we do not, that it is prairie farm rehabilitation, and I think it will be agreed that outside of some very very small areas in British Columbia that term would not apply. Then I went on to say that P.F.R.A. did not even apply to all the prairie provinces; it applied only to the Palliser triangle, which is probably considerably less than half of the prairie provinces, and so it is put there for certain reasons, one of the reasons being that during the time that the lands were owned, operated and controlled from Ottawa they settled those areas in a manner which was not suitable to the districts, and it was thought that Ottawa should do something to change that situation.
That act, as is known, was brought down in 1935 by the government previous to this one. Very little had been done at the time we came in. We changed the act somewhat and went on to administer it from there. It was impossible at that time, and it might be impossible yet, to get the exact terms or anything approaching the exact terms of the P.F.R.A. here, even P.F.R.A. outside on the prairies, and I explained all this to them at this particular meeting, and they said after the meeting was over that they understood why it was not done.
I think that the question that is raised in this article has not especially to do with the P.F.R.A. It has to do with these special votes that we have already considered and passed. There was one there that was especially for British Columbia. It started in the Pemberton flats and went on to operate in other places, more particularly in assisting returned men to settle on lands in the fruit-growing areas in my hon. friend's constituency and elsewhere. We did pay toward those lands out of this special fund. That special fund, in so far as British Columbia is concerned, I think, what is considered to be probably the last vote, is in here now and has already been passed to clean up those expenditures that we had undertaken before. Between now and the next session there may be something else that has to be put in that vote, but there is no intention this session of putting in new amounts to start new projects in connection with that vote.
What they have in mind is, I think, since the lands and resources are entirely under the provinces-and in British Columbia they

have always been-that is a provincial responsibility, and, if they were coming here to ask for assistance, then they should have all the details that are necessary in order to place the case before the government here. Then the matter would be considered on its merits at that time.
I thank the minister for his complete answer. I might mention that the works that were undertaken in the fruitgrowing areas were in Okanagan south.
Yes.

I understand, then, that you would expect that if an application were to be made for further assistance under this act, British Columbia would base that application on a survey of the areas which they were considering at that time.
They would be in a much stronger position if they did.

I have been interested in that question, and I raised the question earlier in the session, as indicated at page 3455 of Hansard this year and again on May 10, when the minister indicated something of what he has said today. I do not want to extend the debate any further, but he did raise a few questions in my mind in his answer, which I suppose is not unnatural. He said, as I recall it, that the reason for non-extension was that certain sections were settled in British Columbia that were not suitable to Ottawa. The area about which I spoke earlier in the session was the lower mainland of British Columbia, which was certainly suitable for agriculture but which required particular work.
Later he went on to say that the reason why it is not extended is that lands and resources have been under the provinces, and these have been under the province of British Columbia, ever since confederation. I am satisfied that lands and resources are under each of the provinces. Today we have the P.F.R.A. in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and those provinces have control of their lands and resources. I cannot agree with the argument of the minister when he makes that particular statement.
I wish to ask him, though, as he has perhaps indicated that this is not going to be extended this year, has he not received a request from the British Columbia government as outlined by the member for Kootenay West and as outlined by the minister himself, for an extension of this particular service under the special act that the minister cited a few moments ago, asking that special consideration be given to the lower mainland of British Columbia, more particularly to the section of

the Mud bay diking area and the Colebrook diking area and the others raised earlier this session?
All I can say is that there have been applications made and that so far the government here has not been prepared to spend money on those projects.

Is the reason for it included in the two reasons mentioned just a few minutes ago, namely that the areas are not settled in a way suitable to the wishes of Ottawa or because the provinces have controlled all lands and resources since confederation?

I did not understand that I said a few moments ago that it was because they were properly settled or not properly settled. If I did, I want to withdraw it because I did not intend to say that. The reason I gave was that the lands and resources are under the provinces. I think my hon. friend misunderstood what was said with regard to the P.F.R.A. area. Those lands and resources were not under the province-either the province of Alberta or the province of Saskatchewan-when those provinces were set up. They were settled from Ottawa until 1931. Practically all the land in those areas had been homesteaded. All that were fit to homestead were homesteaded before that time. So it was decided here over 20 years ago -21 years ago this month, to be exact-to make some expenditures in that P.F.R.A. area because of the past history of it, and that past history does not apply any other place in Canada. All the other lands were under the control of the provinces right from the time they went into confederation.

I fully recall when the provinces received their provincial autonomy in respect of lands and resources and that it was in 1931, because I lived in Alberta at that time. But it seems to me that P.F.R.A. came into effect a while after that period. Was it not about 1934?
Then am I to gather that P.F.R.A. was instituted in compensation for or in lieu of the fact that from 1905 to 1931 the provinces did not have control of their natural resources?

I would not say it was in compensation. It was realizing the fact that the people had been put on land where they could not earn a living. They were in the drought area. It was realized that there were 1 million people settled there and that a very considerable part of them were having some difficulties on account of the fact that drought prevailed there. The Prairie Farm

Rehabilitation Act was set up for the purpose of trying to alleviate their position and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was set up to take care of them in the meantime. I have one final question, or at least I hope it is final. Has the department any particular question on which they are making a decision in respect of the extension of this special grant to the province or this special allowance that is being considered, but not at this time? I understand we passed it earlier. In other words, at this time is any consideration being given to any project in British Columbia that the government might assist in?

No. The position is that when we went into the Pemberton flats and had this vote set up for the purpose of taking care of the situation, the settlers in the Pemberton flats were returned men of the first war. They had been put on the land by the federal government. They had been put on land in that area which, as matters turned out, was flooded periodically. The stream in question, namely the Pemberton river which flows through that area, overflowed its banks. If even a tree fell into the river it started a dam to form from the silt that came down from the mountains, and started the river running in through these men's farms. When we went there first, these men could not work their farms at all in the summer months because the river had spread across their farms. We undertook to dike that river so that their lands would be safe. We did that because they were returned men who were put on the land by the federal government. We carried out that project at considerably greater cost than any of us thought would be involved when we started. Then we took on a similar thing down in the Okanagan district for returned men of the second war. They were largely sons of returned men of the first war. The fathers lived down on the flats near the river. This was at Penticton. There is an area above that on the higher lands on which the sons who came back from this war wanted to settle. We joined up with the Department of Veterans Affairs and the provincial government in making it possible for them to settle there.
Then the other project that was proposed was at Kamloops and it also had a percentage of returned men on it. But eventually we came to the time when, because of the discussions that were going on with regard to

the marketing of apples and the marketing of fruit in general, we could not take the position from here that we were going to extend the production of the crop in British Columbia, and that any responsibility for that action would have to be taken by the provincial government. From the answer I have received, Mr. Chairman, I fully realize that the minister did not answer the last question I put to him. He has given a fine historical background of the present condition to which I have referred.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that if I did not answer it, I intended to do so, because I said this. We said definitely to the British Columbia government that, under no circumstances, will we take responsibility for saying that a change should be made in the farming operations in British Columbia, that such a thing will have to be done by the provincial government and that we will consider the question as to whether we will support it. The point I wish to make is that the district about which the minister is speaking is the apple-growing district. I am not interested in the apple-growing district because apples are not the chief crop, by any means, in the area which I represent and the area about which the minister of agriculture for the province of British Columbia wrote to this minister, as I understand it, asking for an extension. The province of British Columbia apparently has changed its mind in respect of this question which the minister has explained so well. But I am more particularly interested in this matter: What consideration is going to be
TMr. Gardiner.]
given in future and what consideration must be brought to the government's attention if there is going to be any extension? Is it going to be necessary, for instance, that the province of British Columbia prove to this government that there are war veterans in these areas or that the major number of the farms are operated by war veterans? Is that one of the underlying reasons behind the extension of P.F.R.A. or the special grant, or is it just a matter of application by the provincial government? I should like to know,-and I am satisfied my province and more particularly the farmers would- how they are ever going to be able to get assistance from the federal government. We had the mudflats flooded, the dikes went out. I think the provincial government spent some $10,000 in assisting the farmers there. I do not know what the federal government did, if anything. We have each of these diking areas, as I mentioned,-and I do not wish to have to repeat this-which are growing vegetables or used generally as a market-gardening area of British Columbia. That is the finest part of it, at least on the lower mainland, and it is most important that these people get some assistance. Has it been established to the satisfaction of the federal government and the provincial government alike that this is entirely a provincial responsibility? Are they agreed? If so, then I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the house.
That is the case.
That is, it has been definitely established between the two governments it is a provincial responsibility.

That is not only the best farming area in British Columbia but it is the best farming area in Canada and the best farming area in the world that I know anything about. The lands were originally owned and operated by the province. They are entirely under the administration of the province. We are not assisting in that kind of thing anywhere else in Canada, so we do not assist there.

Certainly, it is not my intention to hold up these estimates, but in view of the remarks that have just been made by the hon. members for the Kootenays, and since that suggestion was made to the minister, I want to say that we in this group also have suggested on various occasions that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act be extended to take in all of Canada. take over flood control, conservation and rehabilitation. There are just as many places in eastern Canada as in western Canada that should not be farmed, as the minister well knows. I think probably this whole question could be worked out in co-operation with the provinces and would go quite far towards working out flood control, conservation and rehabilitation of land that is not suitable for agricultural purposes.

Mr. Chairman, at this time I want to express the support of the C.C.F. group and the C.C.F. government of Saskatchewan for an immediate start on the building of the Saskatchewan dam.
The Minister of Agriculture still has an item in the estimates for $500,000 entitled "South Saskatchewan river project". The minister has kept this thing alive in the press and in the house for only one purpose, and that is to mislead the people of western Canada into thinking that he or the government has some intention in the near future to do something about this project. Although the Minister of Agriculture and other colleagues of his in the cabinet at every election campaign for the last 10 years or more have dangled this before the people of Saskatchewan, nothing has been done about it. One excuse after another has been used. In the 1945 federal election campaign and in the 1949 federal election campaign, the line was, we are making surveys, we believe it will be in the national interest, elect us and we will be prepared to proceed with the building of the South Saskatchewan river project. But in spite of all the promises nothing has been done. Instead of getting ahead with the project we are going back.
The minister has taken the attitude over the years, until very recently, that the federal government was prepared to build the project. Now they are trying to slough off some of the cost on the provincial government without any clear commitment that they are prepared to go ahead with the project. The Prime Minister has set himself in opposition to this project. He has asked the people of Canada to produce hundreds of millions of dollars for the St. Lawrence seaway, for projects in other parts of Canada-

Do you disagree with that?

The Minister of Agriculture, of course, knows that perfectly well. When from time to time we ask the Minister of Agriculture questions on the orders of the day about the South Saskatchewan river project and when the Prime Minister is in his seat, the Minister of Agriculture is not true to his normal form when he is prepared to stand up and make a statement quickly and in a clear voice, and debate the issue if necessary; he slumps back in his seat, looks at the Prime Minister, worried. Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I had been saying that the Prime Minister of this country has told us time and time again that as far as he is concerned building the South Saskatchewan river dam is not in the national interest. The people of Saskatchewan resent that attitude very much because they feel they are entitled along with the other provinces in Canada to a share in the beneficial public works that are inaugurated in this nation. They resent it, too, because they believe the South Saskatchewan river project is one that is very definitely in the national interest because it is important to a large geographic area and because a large irrigation project such as the South Saskatchewan dam would mean the irrigation of some 500,000 acres of land. This would assist in stabilizing agriculture in western Canada, would save the provincial government undertaking fodder and seed measures from time to time and would go a long way toward stabilizing the whole economy of that region and subsequently the economy of the nation.
In spite of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture knows full well it is the Prime Minister and others of his colleagues in the cabinet who are standing in the way of the South Saskatchewan river project the minister does not hesitate to make public statements that are misleading, and not in accordance with the facts. As a matter of fact the Minister of Agriculture has attempted to transfer to the government of Saskatchewan the blame for no progress being made on the South Saskatchewan river dam. He went out in his recent Saskatchewan election campaign and not only attempted to blame the Saskatchewan government for the delay of the federal government but he came rather close to using political blackmail when he said that as long as the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan, Mr. C. M. Fines, occupied that post, as far as he, the Minister of Agriculture, was concerned, there would be no development of the South Saskatchewan river project.
The Minister of Agriculture made other statements as reported in the Regina Leader-Post of June 12 under the heading "Gardiner Blames Fines for Delay", and said that the

federal government was prepared to pay 75 per cent of the cost and the province had refused to pay the other 25 per cent.
In case it might be said that I am not quoting from the press report correctly I shall quote the article. The first paragraph reads as follows:
Estevan (staff)-Speaking in support of Jim Cinnamon, Liberal candidate for the Souris-Estevan constituency, agriculture minister James G. Gardiner, at the Canadian Legion hall Monday, blamed provincial treasurer, C. M. Fines for the delay in building the South Saskatchewan river dam. Mr. Gardiner said the dam was a provincial matter-
Listen to this.
-and except for the matter of costs and size of the project, was no different from the proposed dam for Long Creek. He said the federal government had agreed to pay 75 per cent of the cost and that would leave $20 million for the provincial government to find.
As soon as the premier of the province of Saskatchewan saw this report in the Regina Leader-Post he immediately sent the following wire to the Prime Minister under date of June 14, 1956:
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
Rt. Hon. James G. Gardiner has stated publicly at Estevan June 11 that federal government prepared to pay 75 per cent of the cost of South Saskatchewan river project. Saskatchewan government prepared to accept this offer if it is made with full authority of federal cabinet. Please confirm.
T. C. Douglas.
Of course, the answer was that the Minister of Agriculture was not speaking for the federal government when he said they were prepared to begin the project if the Saskatchewan government would produce $20 million.
Who made that reply?
The Prime Minister made the reply that he was not prepared to start the South Saskatchewan river dam.
I mean what was the reply to the telegram that was sent by the premier to the Prime Minister?
The Prime Minister made the reply-
Certainly he made a reply and he did not say what you are saying.
He made the reply that there would be no start made on the South Saskatchewan river project.

speechtext: Read it.
Read the telegram.

speechtext: Ah, that is different.

Honourable T. C. Douglas,
Premier of Saskatchewan,

Re your telegram of South Saskatchewan project I understand Mr. Gardiner's speech to which you refer contained no statement of any federal offer but was mainly recapitulation of portion of his letter to you of January 10, 1955 concerning costs attributable to power and statement that provincial government had never proposed to pay fully and promptly for these power costs. I do not believe this is the time to try to work out arrangements by telegram on this important project.
Louis St. Laurent.
Well, the Prime Minister was a little shifty in that telegram, too, but of course the Saskatchewan election had not yet taken place. The Prime Minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the two questions is a negative one. No decision has yet been made that the government would take the responsibility of recommending that project as one that is in the national interest.
The Prime Minister has shut the door on the South Saskatchewan river project but the Minister of Agriculture does not hesitate to go out to Saskatchewan-
The Prime Minister said the government has taken no decision.

This is the question:
Has the federal government now decided that the building of the South Saskatchewan dam would be in the national interest?
The Minister of Agriculture knowing that no decision had been made to build the project-as a matter of fact knowing that decision after decision had been made not to build the project-said in Saskatchewan,

according to the Regina Leader-Post, that the federal government had agreed to pay 75 per cent of the cost and this would leave $20 million for the provincial government to find.
I would like to learn from the Minister of Agriculture whether or not the government at this time has decided to proceed with this very valuable and important work?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
No. I have asked the Minister of Agriculture whether the government-
When you get all through I will answer all that you are saying; go ahead.
We would like to hear from the Minister of Agriculture an explanation for the kind of antics in which he was engaging a few weeks ago.
Are you all finished?

If the
minister needs to be smoked out perhaps a few more blasts at him will accomplish that fact. I confirm what the hon. member for Assiniboia has said. The minister took the opportunity to go down to my constituency during the election-
No, he wouldn't do that!

-and
once more he held out a carrot for the people of my province before the election. Of course, as hon. members of this house know full well, he was not successful in his attempt because we had the good fortune to elect the C.C.F. candidate, a young man who is a student of economics, and he is now sitting in the legislature there.
We won by 300 votes in your constituency and that is what is worrying you.

That is all right. It is pretty understandable why the Liberals in this house are particularly touchy on this question because it has been their practice during provincial elections and sometimes during federal elections to go out and try to convince the people of Saskatchewan that this government intends to do something about this very valuable project. That has been the history of this matter before every election. The minister in particular has indicated that he was in favour of this very valuable project in order that the people of Saskatchewan might assume that the federal government had some intention of going ahead with the construction. In spite of the fact that for years the provincial government has in my opinion upped their agreement in

Supply-Agriculture
respect to the cost of this project the federal government still reneges and refuses to take any action in the matter.
I agree with the hon. member for Assini-boia that the time has come for the federal government to really take definite action. I do not think it is satisfactory for the Prime Minister to be the only one needing to be convinced. I believe the people of the province have the right to ask the Prime Minister to make up his mind. I know full well that when the St. Lawrence seaway project was mooted in this house I was astounded with the rapidity and agility with which the government undertook the project. I supported it because I thought it was in the interests of Canada, but I do not think politics should be played with this matter or that there should be discrimination against the people of Saskatchewan just because they happen to have a government which the Liberal government here in Ottawa does not favour. As I indicated this morning in respect to flood damage -I think this is almost a comparable situation-in that case this government has given only a mere pittance of $60,000 in connection with another disaster in the province. Now in connection with this particular matter they will not come up and give a single dollar.
I might say further that it astounded some of us when the St. Lawrence seaway project was broached in this house that no argument was offered that the rich province of Ontario was going to be subsidized to the extent of $30 million annually in the way of power. That will be the result of that project. We were not unhappy about it and we went right along with it, but in this case where it has been proved by surveys which have been made to be a worth-while project we think there should be action by the federal government.
Carried.

Let me
say to hon. members that I have sat here for some weeks without rising from my seat. If the hon. member would like to go home, let him buy his ticket and leave. We have some important things to discuss and I intend to discuss this matter.
On May 17, 1955, there was a motion before this house for the construction of the South Saskatchewan river project. I recall that on that occasion every Liberal member from Saskatchewan voted against the immediate construction of that project. The Minister of Agriculture sees fit to go out and criticize the provincial government for not being ready to do this or that, as he did on the occasion I indicated this morning. But he was completely wrong in respect to

flood assistance and the same with this project. The Saskatchewan government has been ready at all times to undertake this on any fair basis that the federal government will agree to. On May 17, 1955 when this motion was before the house every last Liberal member from the western provinces voted against it. The hon. member for Rosthern, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek all voted against it, as did the Minister of Agriculture. The only reason the minister could give for having voted against it was that it was a vote of non-confidence in 'he government.
If we had more help from western Liberal members on this matter we might get somewhere. I know it has been the usual thing for the Minister of Agriculture to say in the west, "Send us a few more Liberals if you want to get something done on the prairie provinces." They have half a dozen more of them here now but I do not see any more support for this worth-while project.
I do want to point out that we feel there has been an injustice done in respect to this worth-while project. The 1953 survey -I might note that that was an election year-carried on by the federal government was an intensive survey. A report was made to this government. There again the only person who needed convincing was the Prime Minister. I suggest that the time has come when this government should take some action and not leave this matter dangling in the air. I shall be interested to hear the comments which the minister will make when I sit down. I say once again that when he spoke at Estevan in my constituency he led the people to believe that the government had changed its mind and something would be done on this project.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot let these remarks go by without making an answer although I hesitate to take up the time necessary to give a full answer. I think I shall read from the same paper from which my hon. friend quoted a few minutes ago in order to place that answer on Hansard. I quote from the Regina Leader-Post of June 18, 1956, as follows:
Mr. Gardiner said he had made the statement often that the South Saskatchewan river project was definitely a provincial responsibility no different from the situation at Estevan where the provincial government contemplated a dam and reservoir.
"When it undertakes construction of the program at Estevan, which it should, the provincial government admits that responsibility. It is understandable, however, that because of the greater cost of the S.S.R. dam, the province should seek financial support from Ottawa," he said.
"This possible support has been discussed at meetings between the province and me, usually

under the chairmanship of Premier Douglas, always after a full discussion with my colleagues in council.
"The provincial government agreed that if the federal government would undertake to construct the dam, which it was estimated would cost $80 million, the former would pay 25 per cent of the cost," he said.
This would relieve the federal government of any charge that it was paying for power for the province provided the province also paid for the penstocks as part of the power plant. (Penstocks are the pipes in the dam carrying water to the turbines.)
However, Mr. Gardiner said, his government had stated that agreement on these points did not commit it to an expenditure of 75 per cent of the cost of the dam and reservoir.
"Prime Minister St. Laurent has always maintained he is not yet convinced the dam is sufficiently in the national interest to justify federal investment of $60 million. The provincial government has not considered it sufficiently in the interests of the people of Saskatchewan to offer to pay more than 25 per cent", he said.
"Mr. Fines has from the beginning questioned whether it would be in the provincial interest to pay even 25 per cent of the costs. In 1950 he questioned whether the province should pay any part of it. Eventually in 1954 and 1955 he went along with proposal it might pay 25 per cent provided the dam was built with federal money and the province was allowed to pay its share with earnings from power after the dam was completed."
Mr. Gardiner said he refused to accept Mr. Fines proposal because it would not be acceptable to the federal government and it would be indirectly subsidizing power development. He offered an alternative: that the provincial government pay its 25 per cent as the work progressed by assigning $2 million each year for ten years from the revenues it was entitled to under the tax rental agreement with Ottawa.
"Mr. Fines took the position he would not be able to finance the province under those conditions," Mr. Gardiner said.
"I asked him then if he could pay half and give provincial treasury bills payable over 20 years for the balance."
This was the only proposal he ever made without first consulting the government, Mr. Gardiner said, and Mr. Fines stated he could not agree to it.
"I was very pleased he had turned it down when I returned to Ottawa and found it would not have been acceptable there either," he said.
At this point, Mr. Gardiner said, he arranged meetings between committees of the two governments and was present at them on the invitation of the Prime Minister. Both Mr. Douglas and Mr. Fines never made any suggestion they were prepared to make any change in their attitude toward paying for the penstocks, he said
"I still contend it will be necessary either that Mr. Fines change his mind or we get a new provincial treasurer if we are to get consideration of an early decision on the dam."
That is the statement that was made. My hon. friend says that the Prime Minister has definitely said, "We are not going to build the dam." The Prime Minister has never said any such thing. Each time that the questions have been asked in this house, they have been to the effect "Is the government now prepared to proceed?" and the Prime Minister has said no to that question,
Supply-Agriculture
but he has never said no to the possibility of the South Saskatchewan dam project being carried out if terms satisfactory to both governments can be arrived at at some time.
As has been stated by my hon. friend, no one questions the fact that I have always advocated the dam. I still advocate it and I am going to continue to advocate it, no matter what position either he or anyone else takes on it. I think it is in the interests of Saskatchewan if it is not in the national interest, and I am still open to conviction on that point, but whether it is in the interests of all Canada or not I know it is in the interests of Saskatchewan and I want to say that if I were head of the government of Saskatchewan today I would build the dam. I should like to know why the government of the province of Saskatchewan is not prepared to come right out and say, "We will spend even more than 25 per cent; we want the dam built", and try to convince the rest of Canada that they are so much interested in building it that the rest of Canada should help to the greatest extent possible.
Would the minister permit a question? Did you permit the Alberta government to pay in toto for the dam that was built there?
We insisted on the Alberta government agreeing to pay dollar for dollar what we pay, and that is quite a different thing from paying 25 per cent.
In Alberta there was a division dollar for dollar on the whole project but not for the dam itself.

There was a division of SOSO in the expenditure on the irrigation project that is based upon the dam, but the dam in Alberta is solely an irrigation dam. It has nothing to do with power, nothing to do with supplying water to communities; it is purely an irrigation dam. There was that arrangement made as between the Alberta government and the federal government.
When the Minister of Agriculture was engaged in so-called negotiations with the cabinet of Saskatchewan, he was not under the instructions of this government to discuss the terms of an agreement.

That is an absolutely false statement and it is only based on the remarks of a gentleman who has all the files in his possession in Regina, and I have them all before me on this desk, and they are before members of this house, and it can be proven from those files that every discussion that I had in Regina with the government was first under discussion with the federal government here. The only time I departed

Supply-Agriculture
from the undertakings given at cabinet as to the things I was to discuss was the incident I mentioned where I suggested that they pay only half the amount and give bonds spread over 20 years to pay the other half.

Then the statement of the minister is wholly and completely inaccurate and false. I am not the one to throw the word "false" into this debate at any time. I do not use that term, as far as members of this house are concerned, but when the accusation is used at me I do not hesitate a moment to throw it back. When the Minister of Agriculture entered into these negotiations with the cabinet of Saskatchewan, he had not the authority and was not under instructions from the federal government to conclude and sign an agreement.

Yes, and the provincial government understood that from every letter written to them; every time I met them that was made absolutely certain, that there could be no undertaking that it was an agreement until such time as the proposed agreement was ready for signature.

When the agreement was ready for signature, there was no signature from the federal government. The minister was out there engaged in loose talk and without authority from the federal government, from the cabinet, to sign an agreement. But I am really astounded at his statement that if he were premier of Saskatchewan today he would be prepared to place the total burden of building the south Saskatchewan project on the economy of Saskatchewan itself-
I did not say that.

-while other parts of Canada were getting many of their projects aided by the federal government, and I am glad and proud that the government of Saskatchewan has said to the Minister of Agriculture that neither he nor anyone else will lead Saskatchewan into signing an agreement that is not on the same general terms as similar agreements signed by other provincial governments with the federal government.
The words of my hon. friend have made it necessary for me to read something else.
He has a lot of files.

The hon. gentleman says
that I made the statement that were I premier of Saskatchewan I would be prepared to build the dam and charge it all up to the people of Saskatchewan. I did not say any such thing. I said that if I were premier of the province today I would go ahead with the building of the dam, and I am quite sure that

if I were premier of the province today, in the light of what our friends in the opposition have said and even in the light of what my hon. friends in the C.C.F. party have said -I do not expect they will ever be at the head of the government here, but they feel there is a possibility of that-and after all they have said, there is no question that if they were here they would pay part of the cost. There is no question that if the opposition were here they would pay part of the cost, and if proper arrangements are made I think there is no question that any government would pay part of the cost. If I were premier of the province of Saskatchewan I would go ahead with that idea in mind, not the idea that this is a responsibility of the federal government and that they ought to do it, which was the beginning of my hon. friend's speech this afternoon, that some time or other I had said that we would do this and therefore, he says, we ought to go ahead and do it.
Hear, hear.

Even if I had said that, which I did not, I am not the whole government of Canada, and I am quite prepared to admit this. There are others who have something to say about this, but in order to refute what has been said I am going to read the last letter that went to the premier of the province of Saskatchewan signed by myself.
What is the date?

January 10, 1955.
Dear Mr. Douglas:
I have your letter of January 3, 1955-
This is the letter that I was reading at Estevan, by the way.
-and in turn am somewhat surprised that you have returned to the position taken in your letter of June 16 when you state:
"If and when the federal government has decided to proceed with the dam we will be glad to discuss with you or with the federal cabinet any details which require clarification."
You will recall that taking that position in June resulted in a discontinuance of discussions between you and me until November 3, 1954. The reopening of those discussions was only made possible by your letter of August 24, in which you stated:
"However the government of Saskatchewan is quite prepared to give consideration to a proposal from the government of Canada setting forth the share of the cost it thinks the government of Saskatchewan should assume, whether or not the proposal is accompanied by an undertaking to construct the dam." I did indicate to you in my letter of August 31, that I had asked Mr. L. B. Thomson to renew discussions with your government. The basis upon which Mr. Thomson renewed those discussions was a draft revised up to September 9th, 1954, which contained the proposal that Saskatchewan pay all costs related to the generation and transmission of power at the main damsite and that Saskatchewan pay 25 per cent of the total cost of the dam which was indicated

as approximately $80,000,000 as work proceeded and did not include the cost of the penstocks which it had already been proposed the government of Saskatchewan should provide for.
Before we were able to arrange a further conference, you wrote the Prime Minister on September 22, 1954, and in that letter stated:
"I would be very glad to go to Ottawa to discuss this matter with you and your colleagues if you can indicate a suitable time for an appointment. . .	. I feel that this is an opportune time to
review the question of commencing construction of the South Saskatchewan dam."
The Prime Minister replied on September 29, to say:
"If we can come to the conclusion it should be proceeded with, we will not have any serious difficulty in working out the right kind of an agreement with your government. I note that you would be prepared to come to Ottawa for further discussions whenever it might seem that such discussions would expedite a decision,"
That the dam should be proceeded with.
With regard to the question of whether I was discussing this matter under the knowledge of the government:
The Prime Minister indicated in the same letter that I planned to bring the matter before the government of Canada and in commenting on this in your letter of October 5, 1954 you write:
"However, I feel that before any decision is made by your government we should have an opportunity of presenting to your cabinet some of the reasons why we think the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam is in the national interest."
My hon. friends say I have not been discussing this matter with the government. I have nothing from the government. The letter continues:
The Prime Minister replied on October 15th that I would meet you in Saskatchewan shortly and on my return and after a report had been received "we will then let you know if this will appear to us to be an opportune time to ask you to come and meet a committee on the cabinet."
This correspondence resulted in my arranging a meeting with you and other members of your government on November 3rd, 1954. It was immediately contended by Mr. Nollet at that meeting that if the provincial government were going to pay the cost of the penstocks, the federal government should lessen the provincial cost by paying for part of the irrigation cost. I maintained that would result in Canada indirectly paying for power and I was sure the government would not agree.
It was then suggested by some one of your government that 25 per cent of the cost would more than cover all power costs, including the penstocks. I made inquiry and was told that this question had been raised in discussions between officials but had not been discussed with the federal government because the estimates of cost of the penstocks had not yet been determined. I stated I was bound by the conditions of my letter of June 8th, 1954, and that this question should be left for further discussion when the officials had reported.
When we met on December 1, I opened by saying this would be my last appearance personally to discuss the South Saskatchewan river dam with the Saskatchewan government. If any further discussions were necessary after I reported back to Ottawa, I thought they could best be carried on between committees of the two governments, as
Supply-Transport
suggested by you. The same condition of uncertainty existed on the cost of the penstocks because estimates were not available. Since then reports have been made by officials which would indicate that to include 75 per cent of the cost of penstocks in federal payments would result in the federal government subsidizing in some degree your "development of hydro-electric power." I submit, therefore, that it must be agreed by the province that the penstocks are their responsibility if we are to proceed to a consideration of' national interest without further discussion.
The two conditions set out in my letter of June 8th, 1954, which was a statement of government policy, were:
"First, it must not directly or indirectly or in effect subsidize in any degree your development of hydroelectric power.
"Second, we must be able to show that the making of this large federal contribution is in the national interest."
As indicated above if the cost of the penstocks included in your 25 per cent payment, your development of hydroelectric power will be subsidized by Canada and therefore must be opposed. The question of responsibility for the cost of the penstocks must be settled before the government of Canada can know what their contribution will be.
Our discussions on November 3rd, 1954, the recent report of the officials on the costs of the penstocks, and my discussion with members of the federal government convince me that it is necessary to have a council meeting such as was stated in my letter of December 22nd, 1954, and that before it will be possible to arrive at a favourable decision on the matter of national interest, it will be necessary to try to come to agreement on the question of responsibility for payment of costs of penstocks and provision for the payment of the province's costs. These agreements can only be reached, if at all, through the meeting in Ottawa of committees of cabinet representing the two governments.
Yours sincerely,
James G. Gardiner.
That is the final letter; and as a result of the writing of that letter I arranged between the premier of Saskatchewan and the Prime Minister for a meeting of those two committees. Those two committees did meet. I was present at the meetings and the discussions end there, all of which my hon. friends will find when they read the record of what was said in the election showing that the statements made that are being brought forward here this afternoon are statements that did not conform with the facts.
