speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.
The hon. member for Danforth is on his feet.

I have been trying to catch your eye, Mr. Chairman.

Supply-Transport
He is easy to see.

There are a couple of items in the estimates of the Department of Transport that I should like to touch upon. One is the railway grade crossing fund and the other has to do with the Canadian National Railways. Both of these matters come under the supervision and control of the Minister of Transport although he does not have anything to do directly with the operation of them.
Last year when the government implemented the report of the board of railway commissioners they increased the railway grade crossing fund from $1 million to $5 million. There was also a revision of the percentage that the railways and the municipalities would receive. This revision was to relieve the railways and the municipalities who were hard pressed, so under it the municipalities would pay 25 per cent, the railways would pay 15 per cent and the grade crossing fund would absorb the remaining 60 per cent of the cost of crossing protection. The board was also given authority to make grants towards the reconstruction and improvement of some of the present installations up to the extent, I think, of $150,000, and particularly in cases of grade separation. As was mentioned last year, the amount of the fund was increased from $1 million to $5 million.
At the time the increase was made we in this party, and I think the majority of the opposition, expressed the opinion that the amount, while it was large, was still inadequate to take care of the situation with which we were confronted. According to the over-all picture presented last year by the board of transport commissioners, it would take somewhere in the neighbourhood of $700 million and about 33 years to take care of this situation, which we all agree is deplorable, and there would only be 1,400 grade separations completed in that time. Thirty-three years is practically one-third of a century. At the same time, while we are trying to improve the situation there is bound to be an increase in the number of level crossings. At the present time, there is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 33,000 level crossings in the Dominion of Canada, and I believe there are 29,600 that are what we would call unprotected crossings. This would leave 3,400 protected crossings in Canada, and that would include the grade separations. The program that the board outlined in connection with grade separations, meaning overpasses and underpasses or subways, would leave a great deal to be done after it was completed.

The annual report of the board of transport commissioners was just received the other day so there was not very much time to go over it and analyse it. It was a very comprehensive report. This report covers the situation up to December 31, 1955, but covers the grade crossing fund only up to the end of March 31, 1955. A great many of the reports we receive in this house are compiled on the same basis, so they are a year behind when we receive them and almost useless. We are discussing something that is past and gone; we are really not up to date. I think the departments would be well advised if they would try to rectify this situation so that we could have reports that were up to date. If they cannot give us the information up to the end of March 31 of the present year, they could at least bring it up to December 31 of the previous year. At the moment, these figures are not much good because, in this particular case, you are discussing a report of the board of transport commissioners on the grade crossing fund which only goes up to March 31, 1955, which is a year and some few months away from the time we are discussing, perhaps the government could look into the matter to see if something could not be done toward improving this condition.
In this report the board has not given complete figures for the year 1955; they have not brought the figures up to date from the time the board made its report in 1954. However, the statistics on accidents have been brought up to date as of December 31,1955, and tabled in February, 1956, and comparisons are made with the years 1951-54. The number of accidents for this year is given as 510, and that is about the highest year in the table when compared with 1951, when it was 490. There were 20 more accidents this year than in the previous highest year. According to the board's report there were only 116 new installations of automatic protective devices last year, and there were 74 existing protective devices which were improved upon. Some progress was shown, therefore, but there were also 181 new crossings opened and 31 closed, while there were four highway diversions. Contributions from the fund amounted to $1,219,613, and the projects approved for construction 1955-but that does not necessarily mean starts were made on the work-were 59 railway bridges; 31 overhead bridges and subways; 89 protected crossings with flashing lights and bell; 27 electrically controlled gates and flashing lights. This is all very good, but it does not give us the picture of whether or not there has been any over-all progress in the elimination of these level crossings. I think we are probably slipping back, as we have been

from year to year. The situation is getting beyond us. I do not see anything about the completion of grade separations, so I can only speak of my own knowledge and I know that the Woodbine avenue subway in the city of Toronto was completed last year. It is a very great improvement.
I assume that there must have been a great many requests to the board for work to be undertaken. Naturally, that would follow because when you increase the fund by about 400 per cent you are going to have demands for some work to be done. However, it all hinges upon just how far the municipalities, the railway companies and the provinces can go. If they have not the funds available to keep up with the money that is provided by the federal government, naturally the program is going to be slowed up. This causes us to ask ourselves if we are attacking the problem from the right angle. Although the fund was increased to $5 million last year that increase was not effective until after the house prorogued and therefore there could not be much spent from the fund and it did not really become operative until after the first of the year.
This year's report of the progress that has been made will probably give us a better picture of what has been accomplished with the $5 million that has been set aside. I do not think we have to wait for the report; I think we can probably decide that it will not be adequate to take care of the situation in the future. The board has mentioned that neither the railways, the municipalities nor the provinces are in a position to take full advantage of the fund that has been placed at their disposal.
When one examines the reports of accidents that have taken place he finds that one thing stands out. There were 510 accidents last year, and 80 per cent of them, or 410-I stand to be corrected on that figure-[DOT] occurred at unprotected crossings. The ratio of accidents at unprotected crossings is the same percentage as at protected crossings. At the turn of the year there was a series of appalling accidents at grade level crossings in the Ottawa district. In the riding adjacent to mine, York-Scarborough, there was an accident right on the borderline on the northeast perimeter of the Danforth riding and the southwest perimeter of York-Scarborough riding. This appalling accident happened there on Christmas day last year.
Scarborough has some 82 grade level crossings of various kinds. Eleven or 12 of them require grade separation, and about 50-odd require what we call protection. Two of them had something done last year. One underpass or grade separation may have been provided. Further applications have been made 67509-446
Supply-Transport
this year to have more projects started, but that does not mean the board is going to grant them. Around the Toronto area, particularly in the Etobicoke area, the accidents are keeping pace with the number that occurred in years gone by.
I should like to refer to the situation in Brockville, which is evident to one as he goes back and forth to Toronto. I do not know whether there have been any accidents there, but it is certainly a miracle if there have not been any. The people in the city of Brockville certainly must be very patient. The roads are blocked there, particularly when there are freight trains in the station, or when a change-over is being made. The length of time the people have to wait for the crossings to be cleared is provoking. It is a wonder that there are not more accidents at those street crossings.
The board of transport commissioners is to be very highly commended for their action in connection with the railway diversion that took place at the St. Lawrence seaway project. The location of the railways there has to be changed, and a good many subways, underpasses or overpasses or whatever you wish to call them, have to be installed. The railways and the department of highways were adamant in their stand that they did not want to undertake the cost; they did not want to foot the bill for putting in new grade separations. The board had the matter before it, and it is to be highly commended on its adamant position. They insisted on having the proper number of subways installed to protect the people.
It was the same old story that we heard at the time of the erection of the union station in Toronto. It stood idle for over ten years for the simple reason that they could not bring the railways to the point where they would construct the grade separations to protect the travelling public in Toronto. The matter finally went before the courts and they were ordered to put them in. The same situation would have prevailed at the St. Lawrence seaway project if the board had not taken a sound and strong attitude. They took the position that grade separations had to be installed to protect life. In my opinion that is one place where the board proved its worth.
Last year the situation had become rather serious because of the deaths on the highways at grade level and other crossings. A board was formed known as the national accident prevention board, of which the former minister of defence was made chairman for a time. He was succeeded by Mr. Ash, who was the chairman of the Ontario safety league. They got off to a rather late

Supply-Transport
start, but they have made some wonderful progress. They followed one of the suggestions made in the board's report last year, that an advisory committee should be formed to assist in overcoming the mounting number of accidents on the highways and at grade level crossings. That is one of the right steps to rectify the situation. Greater effort will have to be made to prevent accidents in the future. Probably some of the expenses connected with that campaign can be drawn from the fund, or provision can be made to use funds from the grade level crossing fund to augment the staff who are working on the prevention of accidents in the future. If that fund were used in this way it would be money well spent.
The task of eliminating grade level crossings is an enormous one. At present not much can be said about accidents at grade level crossings this year. As I said, probably next year we shall have a better opportunity to obtain a more complete and thorough analysis of it than this year.
I should like to deal for a moment with the annual report of the Canadian National Railways. I see from the report that in 1954 the Canadian National Railways had a deficit of $28,758,000. In 1955 they had a surplus of $10,717,000. That looks like a pretty good performance, but there are some observations I should like to make which may throw a less favourable light on it. These are the conclusions I have come to. This surplus was built up from the increased revenue accruing from freight traffic. Four-fifths of the revenue came from freight traffic. Then there was a slight increase in the intercity passenger traffic.
In the intercity service, where the traffic was up a little, the increase was stimulated by a greater effort to secure patronage by an improvement in the speed, service and standards and what they call "specials". I suppose that would be excursions between the cities. However, this was offset by a drop in commuter traffic which was induced by modifications to the suburban service. I suppose by "modifications" they mean there was a decrease in the service that was given.
However, I was intrigued by the reference to the punitive deferral on maintenance. No matter how close the balance is in renewing and replacing, it is not only risky but generally it has dire results. The results are poor plant, faulty equipment and bad service. That is eventually what happens.
Further on in the report mention is made of labour. While there was an increase in wages in the payroll of $794,939 over 1954, there was a staff reduction of 2,366, and this no doubt was brought about by the deferring
of a maintenance plan and by other means of escaping or evading necessary maintenance. Although they say they want to avoid it I think they have walked right into it, because when you take the average annual wage of the employees involved at $3,152, there would be a payroll saving of $7,500,000, which would make up three-quarters of the 1955 surplus. The future will tell whether this was a good operation. In 1955 there were 116,583 employees and in 1954 there were 118,949 employees, which means a decrease of 2,366. The payroll in 1955 was $375,600,000 and in 1954 it was $376,397,939 which is an increase of $797,939. I can only conclude that this is not a good operation.
Another matter I would like to touch upon is one about which a great deal has been said since the first of the year. I am referring to commuter service, particularly as it relates to the railways. I have already referred to the intercity traffic and service and how the railway really concentrated on increasing the patronage and improving the service. I would like to ask what efforts have been made toward improving the lot of the commuting population and increasing the patronage. Of the entire passenger traffic last year 44 per cent was made up of the commuter population.
Perhaps I could approach this matter best by reading from the report of the board of transport commissioners for Canada for the year ended December 31, 1955. I shall refer to an application of the Canadian passenger association for rescission of the board's order No. 75234, dated September 21, 1950, which prescribed commutation fares. An application was brought for an increase in rates, particularly in the Oakville area. This reference appears on page 14 of the report. I do not think the background details are necessary, and I shall begin by reading the following excerpt from the report:
The commutation rates in effect when the application was made in May 1954, were prescribed by the board in 1950 by order No. 75234. The railways in this application sought rescission of that order concurrent freedom to increase commutation rates approximately 100 per cent, half of the proposed increase to be effective immediately followed six months later by the full increase. The application affected a number of areas including the Toronto and Montreal areas and the first hearing was held at Toronto and related to commutation services and fares in that area. Following that hearing the board held in a judgment dated August 4, 1954, that in dealing with commutation services the time had arrived to apply a general rule that a railway is entitled to charge commutation rates at a level that will return at least the railway's reasonable and actual out of pocket cost of furnishing the service concerned and that the railway should not be required by the board to provide or continue to provide commutation services which will not meet that cost. The board thereupon authorized adjustment of commutation rates in the Toronto area as applied

for but subject to the condition that the increases be made effective in three stages, namely approximately 50 per cent of the increase not earlier than September 30, 1954, another 25 per cent not earlier than six months from the date of the first increase and the final portion not earlier than another six months thereafter. Subsequent to that judgment hearings were held in Montreal. The railways submitted that the application if granted would do nothing more than give the railways a fighting chance to recover mere out of pocket costs; also that when rates are shown to be below the compensatory level the board has an obligation to see that they do not remain below that level but that the railway may, in their sole discretion, fix commutation rates at any higher level they wish if such rates are less than the coach class passenger rates and if there is no unjust discrimination. Opposing municipalities did not object to rescission of the 1950 order but maintained that the proposed increase of 100 per cent was excessive and that all the railways need is an increase of 35 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, I should perhaps read the next paragraph because this will have little meaning unless I do.
Your time is nearly up, so you had better get going.

The board held that when the railways on their own initiative and for many years have caused commuter rates to be established in given areas and sought to have them increased the board can quite legally and properly consider with respect to both commuters and the railways the reasonableness of the proposed increased fares and the manner in which they are to be applied; and that on the facts before the board in the present case, it has jurisdiction to prescribe the rates and to fix, determine and enforce just and reasonable commutation rates; that while further evidence and investigation are necessary before final judgment can be rendered, sufficient proof was made to justify the railways putting into force an increase of 50 per cent as it appeared that even if the commuters are given the benefit of every reasonable doubt the revenues with such rates in effect will not exceed the out of pocket costs properly chargeable to commuter service.

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three matters I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport. Perhaps it would eliminate repetition and save time if I referred to them on this item instead of taking them up separately.
First I should like to thank the minister for the attention my riding has received from his department. We appreciate what his 67509-446J
Supply-Transport
department has done during the past four or five years in the way of improving aids to navigation. A great many fog stations have been rebuilt and the equipment modernized, but there is still a great deal more to be done. We need a great many lighthouses, light and whistle buoys and bell buoys, and we trust that the provision of the new supply ship which we hope will be in operation before another year will make it possible to provide these additional aids.
I should like also to express appreciation for the sympathetic consideration I have always received from the senior officials of the department both here and in Newfoundland, and for the efficient manner in which they have dealt with the various problems I have presented to them. Since mine is a coastal riding, hon. members will understand that the Department of Transport plays a vital part in the life of my constituents.
Strange as it may seem, I should like to say a word of thanks to the Canadian National Railways. I am particularly appreciative of their efforts to assist the producers of my province in the marketing of their fish. A recent visit was made by their senior expert on fish tariffs and rates which resulted in the working out of a beneficial freight rate for the fresh fish producers of my riding.
I should like also to thank Canadian National Telegraphs for the various small telephone stations they have established during the past year. One of these stations which was recently established made possible the saving of a human life, which alone justified any expenditure the department might have made, even though it might be a long time before the expenditure will be offset by the revenue received.
I should like to draw to the attention of the minister a Canadian Press report which appeared in the Newfoundland papers of June 6. According to this press report the deficit on the ferry William Carson for the year 1955 amounted to $4,500,000. I do not know how that figure was arrived at, but I assume it resulted from taking item 460 in the amount of $3,496,250 and adding a similar item in the supplementary estimates in the amount of $1,123,830. The publication of this report caused considerable consternation in Newfoundland, when it was thought that the deficit on the ferry operation would amount to such a tremendous figure. I believe there must be some misunderstanding there, and perhaps these figures indicate the deficit on the whole railway operation rather than on the ferry service alone. I would be grateful for any light the minister can

Supply-Transport
throw on this matter, either when he replies on this item or later when we are dealing with item 460.
These figures on the deficit point up a startling fact. The railway operation in Newfoundland is vital to the economy of the province. We are dependent entirely upon the Newfoundland railway and the coastal services to meet our transportation needs.
I would be the last to deprecate what the Canadian National Railways have done to improve the services. They have spent many millions of dollars in improving the roadbed and providing modern and up to date equipment, but in spite of that the service today is relatively worse in comparison to the needs than it was 20 years ago.
The startling fact which I feel should be pointed out to hon. members is that this situation must continue and will worsen as time goes on. In the first place the Newfoundland railway was never built to meet the needs that exist today. In the second place the Newfoundland economy is expanding at such a rapid rate that it never will be possible for the railway to catch up, no matter how many millions of dollars are spent in the future. Even if the present system were converted to standard gauge I do not think it would be adequate. In my opinion what is needed is a completely new transportation system.
I read in the press a few days ago that a survey party was on its way to Newfoundland. The press report did not indicate the scope of the survey to be undertaken, but I submit that a most comprehensive survey is needed. Before we begin to analyze the transportation problem in Newfoundland we must have a very clear picture of what the transportation system should do. It is not just a matter of carrying passengers and goods from one point to another; it is much more than that.
Newfoundland can be divided into three economic subdivisions, each of which is independent of the others. The first function of any transportation system should be to integrate those three economic subdivisions into a single economic unit. Having done that, the second and more important function is to integrate the whole province into the economy of the mainland. Until those two objectives have been achieved Newfoundland will never enjoy the benefits of confederation. We have had seven years' experience, and we know just what we are talking about. We know also that, just as the railway integrated British Columbia into the economy of Canada as a nation, so must the transportation system of the Canadian National Railways do the same for Newfoundland.

I point that out to the minister because there is not another minute to lose. We cannot construct the railway overnight. At best it will take years, possibly five or ten years, to develop a transportation system that will meet the needs. We must remember that our present railway was built when our population was 250,000 people. Today we have a population of 425,000 people, and in 20 or 25 years' time we expect to have a population of over 800,000 people. For these reasons it is important that we begin thinking and planning and working out a solution to this problem now.
The other point to which I wish to draw the attention of the minister is the inadequacy of the coastal services. My riding is a coastal district. The railway touches it only at each end, and in between points from east to west are served by Canadian National Railways coastal boats. This service is very slow. It has been modernized as far as the ships are concerned, with one important exception on which I shall enlarge a little later, but the sailings are much too infrequent for the business needs of the riding.
We all know that communications are the key to economic development. Certainly my riding is one of the "have not" ridings of the whole province of Newfoundland. Economic development cannot take place unless communications are much more improved. There is one particular part of the coastal service about which I want to speak especially, and that is the Placentia bay area. I have been talking about this for the past four years. I have brought it up in the railway committee, and the president of the Canadian National Railways has always assured me that this problem would be taken care of just as soon as the William Carson ferry was completed and put into operation. We waited patiently for a year for the ferry to be built, and now the ferry has been built for a whole year and she is still not in her regular service, and it looks as though it might be another year before that problem is taken care of.
I want to point out to the minister, as I have done to the Canadian National Railways, that even when the ferry goes on her regular schedule across the gulf, the diverting of the S.S. Bar Haven to the Placentia bay service will not solve that problem, because whilst the Bar Haven is a satisfactory ship for one part of the bay, she is certainly not adequate for the other parts. At present this area is served by a cargo vessel. There is nothing wrong with the vessel as a ship, and there is nothing wrong with the captain or the crew; they are the equal of any in the world. I travel with them every year and I enjoy my

trip with them; but I see for myself the conditions under which passengers have to travel and I can tell hon. members that at times, particularly in the fall and winter when the weather is stormy and the days are short, the conditions are indescribable. There is no word that I know that can adequately describe them. If any newspaper like Week End or the Toronto Star wanted a good photo story, I submit they could get one if they sent their photographers down to take a trip on this vessel.
The only way to solve this problem is to construct a vessel especially for this service. That is what the Reid Newfoundland Company did 50 or 60 years ago. The places are the same today as they were then; the geography is the same; the harbours have not changed. They found it necessary to build a ship especially for that service. I have urged that now for the past six years, but my pleas have fallen on deaf ears.
I must say it is almost inhuman to expect these people to go on putting up with this service much longer. There is no other service; they have to take that or leave it. They are not treated as second-class passengers, nor even as fourth-class passengers. I doubt that there are many places in the world where the passengers travel under the same conditions. As I said before, this is no reflection on the captain or the crew; they go out of their way to make the passengers as comfortable as they can. But the ship has only eight berths. Very often it has to carry 40 passengers and the rest have to sit up all night in rough weather, tossing about in what I call indescribable conditions. I urge the minister to use his influence with the Canadian National Railways to tackle this problem without another minute's delay.
In conclusion I should like to remind the minister once again of the plight of the telegraphers in Newfoundland. I referred to them in the debate on the speech from the throne. I have had correspondence about them since, and I understand that some negotiations have been going on with a view to alleviating their conditions.
The situation arises from a change in policy on the part of the Canadian National Railways, replacing the present Morse instruments with a telephone service. The people in the community deplore the telephone service because they say it is not private; the telephones apparently go out of order very quickly and are out of order for a very long time before someone can arrive to get them working again.
The worst part of it, of course, is that the change-over to telephones from Morse instruments is going to result in a reduction in
Supply-Transport
salary for the operators. Most of them are, as I pointed out earlier this session, now existing on meagre salaries of around $100 or $113 per month, and it is almost impossible for them to live and bring up their families on that amount, but they are trying to do so. There is no alternative work there for them. They are employed the full day in a separate office away from their place of residence. They have regular business hours that they must maintain irrespective of the amount of traffic they handle, and there is no opportunity for them to supplement their earnings. It is not a part-time job at all; it is a fulltime job.
This reduction from $100 or $115 down to perhaps $75 or $80 is going to make it impossible for these people to live at all. 1 hope when the minister speaks he may be able to bring us up to date as to what has happened in the meantime, but if developments have not reached that stage yet, I urge upon him to keep this problem in mind and to do his best to have a solution worked out at the earliest possible date.

Some of us are rather concerned at recent developments in freight rates in this country. We have seen, since the end of the war, a great many increases in freight rates. There was a long series of increases from 1948 to March, 1953. We had thought in 1953 that perhaps this series of increases might be ended for a substantial time to come. Those increases were as follows:
April 8, 1948	 21 per cent
June 16, 1950	 20 per cent
February 11, 1952	 17 per cent
January 1, 1953	 9 per cent
March 16, 1953	 7 per cent
That series of increases in freight rates totals 98 per cent. Time and time again it was pointed out before the board of transport commissioners by counsel representing the three western provinces and the maritime provinces, that any increase in freight rates adds immensely to the cost of long hauls, particularly in certain commodities, and that the total effect of any increase in freight rates is to make the burden of freight rates still more unequal in this nation. Any increase in freight rates increases the burden on the freight users of the prairies and the freight users in the maritimes provinces.
When the railways ask for an increase in freight rates and are given one, they have found that they are not able to take the increase they are given and apply it equally to all the traffic they have. They have found that a large part of their traffic is subject to competition, such as water competition and perhaps truck competition. Hence they have been obliged to take the increase that has been granted and apply

Supply-Transport
it to less than all of their traffic. There has been a deterioration in the amount of traffic to which a given freight rate could be applied.
This whole phenomenon has come to be known as attrition, an abrasion of the increase that has been given. It is estimated that for every dollar of increase that is given, perhaps only 60 cents or 70 cents is in fact effective. Each further increase in freight rates therefore adds an additional burden to those manufacturers who must compete by using long freight hauls, and particularly to that of the consumers who have to pay the freight rate, because it is often passed on to them.
I do not think there is any economic justification or any justification from the standpoint of national policy for further increases in freight rates at this time. If anyone will look at the profits of the railway companies over the past few years I believe they will see that while gross revenues at certain times have gone down, the net profits of the railway companies have gone up. The railway companies have been able to make certain savings through dieselization, through increasing freight train speeds and by increasing the size of freight trains. I am convinced that the savings which the railway companies have been able to make render unnecessary any increase in freight rates at this time. If you add in the last increase in freight rates, namely the so-called 7 per cent interim increase, you find that since 1948 freight rates in this country have been increased by the phenomenal figure of 112 per cent, and there does not appear to be any end to it.
From press reports and other statements I have noticed that there has already been an indication that if further wage increases are given those in the non-operating unions, there will subsequently follow increases in freight rates. As a matter of fact, when this 7 per cent interim increase was being considered that thought went through the whole proceeding. The recent application was for a 15 per cent increase. Was consideration given?

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member should realize that this is a matter which is now before the board of transport commissioners. While the hon. member may not be put under any disability as to the consequences of what he says, I think the position is extremely unequal. I am clearly not in a position to debate and discuss a matter which is before the board of transport commissioners and as to which there may be an appeal to the governor in council. I am therefore in the
[Mr. Argue.}
position of being unable to reply to this argument with regard to the proceedings now before the board.
I did not complain, Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member spoke about increases in the past, but when he deals with matters which are currently before the board I am placed in an invidious and unfair position.
An untenable position.

On that point, Mr. Chairman, may I say this. The minister may find himself in a rather difficult position, but the point is not whether the minister or I or any other member of this house may be in a rather difficult position but rather that here is a case where a grave injustice may be done to the freight users and the people of this nation.
Mr. Chairman, this whole question is sub judice at the moment, and it seems to me that it is quite improper to pursue the discussion and deal with such current matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I might point out that it has been decided-see citation 251- that the board of railway commissioners, now the board of transport commissioners, is a court of record. I know that remarks somewhat similar to those which the hon. member is now making were made earlier in the session. At that time the gist of the remarks was not to affect the decision which the board of transport commissioners was making but rather, I think, to make an appeal to the cabinet to exercise certain powers which it had as to deferring or upsetting the decision which the board of transport commissioners had made at that time by way of interim judgment.
The minister is correct in saying that if this matter is still before the board of transport commissioners for decision the argument which the hon. member for Assiniboia wishes to make should be made before that board in an exactly similar manner as if it were a case before the courts. The case would be argued in this house only after the courts had rendered a decision, if it was within the power of this house to take some action to amend the decision.
I think the hon. member for Assiniboia will agree with me as far as I have gone. If he is able to restrict his remarks to any action which he feels the cabinet should or should not have taken on the judgment which has been rendered, I do not think I could interfere with him. But if the purpose of his remarks is to influence a decision which the board of transport commissioners is arriving at, then of course they would be definitely out of order here at this time.

On the question of whether or not the question is sub judice, may I say this. I think it should be pointed out that it is perfectly in order for any member of this house, I take it, as a citizen of this nation or for any other citizen to discuss the question of freight rates any place in Canada, including such places as in the newspapers and on public platforms. I do not feel that we in this house should be relegated to a position inferior to that which may be taken by any other citizen of this nation who is not a member of this house. We can go across this nation, as some of us will, and discuss this very matter.
The second thing I wish to point out is that the case is not now before the board. If I may explain-
The hearing has been set for September.

If I may explain what happened, I should like to do so. They had a nice little cosy meeting of the board of transport commissioners, and they decided that they were not going to have any long, detailed discussion at the present time. Although there was before the board an application for a 15 per cent increase they did not say, "We will wait until this case can be reviewed in its entirety and then a decision can be made". No, they did not say that. They said, "We will give the railway 7 per cent without a hearing, without any consideration". Then there was an adjournment. As the minister points out, the adjournment is now in effect. This particular question is not today being discussed before the board of transport commissioners.

May I suggest that a hearing has been fixed for the month of September. Consequently the issues which my hon. friend seems to want to discuss are before the board at this time. My understanding of parliamentary practice is that it is not the custom to debate issues in the House of Commons, or in fact in any legislative body, which are before the courts. It seems to me that is a sound principle. I have been in the same position as my hon. friend, where I have wished to discuss issues that were before the courts and where the rule has prevented me from doing so. I can say to him that the rule does not stop him from talking about it outside the House of Commons, but certainly the rule and tradition have always been that one does not discuss in the House of Commons or any parliamentary assembly issues that are before the courts.

May I just say a word on this point of order; I presume it is a point of order that has been raised. I believe the
Supply-Transport
minister's contention would be very well taken if in fact the hearings were going on now or if a 7 per cent interim increase in freight rates had not been granted. Now I contend the 7 per cent is history. It is not contingent in any way upon what happens at the September hearings. Consequently, Mr. Chairman, I contend we are quite within our rights in discussing all the issues involved at least within the 7 per cent increase that has been granted. If in the discussion of that 7 per cent we do touch upon the principles involved in connection with it, certainly it would seem to me we would be in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think there is really very little need for the committee or the hon. member for Assiniboia to be in any difficulty. Citation 252, which I am going to read because it is not very long, says:
Matters which have been adjudicated upon by the railway commissioners and taken in appeal to the governor in council cannot be considered sub judice while the appeal is pending, because the governor in council then acts in an administrative and not a judicial capacity, and therefore such matters may be debated in the House of Commons.
The point is that the board of transport commissioners does act in a judicial capacity. The House of Commons acts in a legislative or executive capacity. The member for Assiniboia will agree with me that is not the position of the application for the 15 per cent increase before the board of transport commissioners, the hearing of which has been postponed. The fact that the hearing has been postponed does not mean that it is not before the board of transport commissioners. Therefore I think he did make a specific reference to that application, and such specific references to the application should not be carried on at the present time.
However, a general discussion of freight rates is in order. Any criticism of the action which he may choose to take to offset that increase which has been granted is also in order. With reference to the hon. member's suggestion that this puts a member of parliament in a lower position than a newspaper reporter, there are circumstances under which newspapers can be impeached for contempt of court by attempting to try a case which is before the courts. Of course that is going very far. Hon. members in this house are protected from every sort of action by their parliamentary immunity; therefore I think they have a greater responsibility than others for remaining within the bounds of not discussing matters which are sub judice, and within that general thought I am sure the hon. member for Assiniboia can continue.

I think perhaps I can make my remarks within the bounds you have set by the statement that you have just made,

Supply-Transport
Mr. Chairman. But I would point out, with regard to your reference to the press, and what might be done if this question is discussed in the press that this important economic question will be discussed outside of parliament, and I do not think any action of any kind will be taken.
I think I can keep my remarks within your statement that one can discuss things that have happened in the past, increases that have been made in the past, even though such increases may be only interim. With that in mind, I want to make it quite clear that I believe the 7 per cent interim increase, the thing that has now been done, was wrong. The board of transport commissioners, I feel, made a tragic blunder in providing the 7 per cent increase at the time it was granted without sufficient evidence before the board for anyone to decide whether or not that 7 per cent increase was justified.
It is not a matter that affects only the people of the prairie provinces. The hon. member for Cape Breton South has pointed out on more than one occasion that the people in the maritime provinces are adversely affected by increases in freight rates. The people of British Columbia are adversely affected by any increase in freight rates. I am sure that the hon. member for Kootenay West is much better acquainted than I am with the position of the fruit producers in his province.
It has been stated by the British Columbia small tree fruits association, representing the British Columbia fruit industry, that it is virtually impossible for that industry to absorb further increases in freight rates. This was pointed out before the 7 per cent was granted; that the price of apples has been reduced progressively from $1.32 per box in 1952 down to just 77 cents per box in 1955. They point out that with an increase in freight rates of 7 per cent the industry is going to be placed in economic jeopardy. I believe the government is going to have to take a look at its whole transportation policy to see if some alternative can be found to further horizontal increases in freight rates. Some other measures will have to be adopted.
I notice that those of us who feel that other measures must be adopted are not alone. An organization as powerful and as prominent as the Canadian Manufacturers Association has made a statement that some other system of alleviating the distress of the railways must be found. They have said this:
Thus the law of diminishing returns inexorably asserts itself, and it is becoming increasingly apparent that recourse to means other than a general freight rate increase will ultimately have to be found to maintain the railways in a healthy condition.

I think the government should consider now a type of transportation policy that will include, wherever it may be necessary in order to hold down freight rates, wherever it may be necessary to provide equality of freight rates, a system of subsidies and controls so that this may be brought about. We have already had certain steps taken in that direction. A few years ago we had provided by law a $7 million subsidy paid for the maintenance of the trackage in northern Ontario. The purpose of that $7 million subsidy was to help assist the railways in moving freight over that area, which is considered a relatively barren area. It was the belief of parliament when the $7 million subsidy was granted that it would go a considerable distance toward enabling equalization of freight rates to take place.
I believe it is time now that the government considered the whole question of subsidies for the railways, the whole question of controls, and made certain that out of this government policy two things come about: first, no further increases in freight rates and, second, an equalization of those freight rates now in existence.
May I refer to one other thing that is past history in this country, but which I am fearful may be brought up to date before too long. That is the whole question of whether the railways have the right to charge demurrage on box cars of grain waiting to unload at terminal elevators. This question was decided-
This is again a question which is before the board. Surely my hon. friend is not going to pursue another matter which is under consideration by the board?

Not at all; I am not going to pursue a question that is before the board. I am merely going to make reference to a very wise decision that was made by the board of railway commissioners for Canada on August 15, 1937. Back in the 1930's there was an application before the board for demurrage charges for the unloading of grain at terminal elevators. Great controversy took place at that time as to whether demurrage charges should be allowed to the railway companies. It was decided at that time that while the railway companies might be allowed to charge demurrage on other freight traffic, the question of charging demurrage on grain was an entirely different proposition. In the judgment of that day-and it is an old judgment, dated August 15, 1937-at page 197, I find the following. I think it is something that members in this house might consider. It reads:
I cannot refrain from repeating that I think we should consider the question of western grain

transportation as distinct from the transport of other commodities. While the principle underlying the application of a demurrage charge is sound in respect to rail transportation in general, and should be applied where cars are unreasonably or improperly detained by shippers or by consignees, in my opinion an exception should be made in regard to western grain at terminal points. Parliament seems to have recognized a distinction as between western grain and other transportable commodities not only in the Canada Grain Act, but also in regard to railway rates for the transportation of grain. While ordinary freight rates are subject to the jurisdiction of the board under the provisions of the various sections of the Railway Act, parliament itself enacted maximum rates for the transportation by rail of western grain to the head of the lakes. Subsequently, the board made the same scale of rates effective for shipment of western grain via Pacific ports. I am not aware of similar action by parliament in respect of any other commodity. I think, therefore, that one may well hold that shipments of grain to terminal elevators may be treated as an exception to the general demurrage tariff. For many years, the railways have so treated it, and I can find no sound reason at the present time for altering the method adopted by the railways in the past.
I believe that was a sound and wise decision, Mr. Chairman; I believe it is something that should not be left as a decision of the board of transport commissioners, but rather that the government should adopt it as a matter of policy and bring in a measure to place in the Railway Act of this country a provision which will prevent railway companies from charging demurrage in the unloading of grain.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to enter this debate on behalf of the numerous people who are unable to procure telephone service at this time. The reason I speak on the estimates of the Minister of Transport is that the board of transport commissioners has some little say with regard to the rate charged by the telephone companies across Canada.
A great shortage of telephones existed during the war period, and that is understandable. When the resources of this country were required to fight and win a war it was not realistic to think that telephone service should be given to everyone at that time. The existence of shortages was true with respect to almost every commodity at the end of the war. There were no automobiles; there were no refrigerators; there were no electric stoves; there was none of the things that so many households required at the end of the war. But the telephone system, because of, you might say, a monopoly permitted by this government, is the only industry which, some 11 or 12 years after the war has not caught up with the scarcity which existed then. I would think there are more people wanting telephones today than there were at the end of the war. The telephone companies have not approached their problem in 67509-447
Supply-Transport
a manner that will permit them ever to catch up with the shortage that exists.
The telephone companies give various excuses. I need only to look at my own city to see how they have mismanaged the problem of supplying people with telephones. I do not disagree with government policy. I agree that we cannot have two or three different telephone companies servicing one area, but I do know this. If two companies were permitted to service an area where new houses are being built, there would be salesmen at the doors of those houses before the people moved in, offering them telephones. The companies would not take the position that the house is there and at some time the people are going to have to come to that particular company and beg for a telephone. They would not take the position that the customer has to wait until they decide that now is the time, we shall give him a telephone. They would be out after business, and they would be looking to this tremendous market as a means of earning money.
The thing that I do not understand is why the shareholders of the telephone companies have not explained very clearly to their management that they have done a poor job, that they have done the poorest job of all the companies in the Dominion of Canada that are supplying the needs of the people. There is not an automobile manufacturer that will not give you a car today. There is not a company building refrigerators that cannot give you a refrigerator, or a company manufacturing electric stoves and washing machines that cannot give you a washer or electric stove. You can go out and buy a suit of clothes; you can buy a pair of shoes. You could buy none of these things as you wished at the end of the war; neither could you get a telephone then. You can get these other things today, but you cannot get a telephone.
The telephone companies have looked on the progress of Canada with the most bleak, barren and unimaginative program that was ever presented to the Canadian people. I think it is time the shareholders took a look at their companies and said to the management, "Now is the time to take a new look at the situation, and when you see in a city a couple of hundred houses being built, you get prepared to supply those houses with telephones before they are built, not a year or two years afterwards." They say, "Well, we have not the supplies; we just cannot do it physically."
Let me tell those telephone companies this. They are in the position of a city, only on a much smaller scale. What has to be supplied in a city in which new houses are being built? They have to supply schools, hospitals, sewage

Supply-Transport
capacity and waterworks. I would suggest to those telephone companies that for every dollar they spend on buildings and switchboards the taxpayers of the community have to spend $1,000 to supply schools, hospitals, sewage plants and pumping stations. For every dollar the telephone companies pay for stringing a line to a new section of the city, the city has to pay $1,000 to put down sidewalks, streets, sewers, gutters, storm sewers and all the things that make up the services of a city. When you go to the house owner you will find that to buy his home he spends $1,000 for every dollar the telephone company has to spend to put a telephone in that home. When this huge project is being planned and developed in Canada we have the telephone companies blithely saying that people will have to wait until they are ready to give them telephones. The companies know that people cannot obtain telephones from anyone else.
I think it is time the board of transport commissioners took a look at the telephone companies and said to them, "You have the sole right to service these homes and when you service them you make a profit on it; and we are going to see that as long as there is an application for a telephone in any area that you cannot fill within a week, which is a reasonable period of time, you will have no right to raise your rates in that area."
If this were done I am quite convinced the management of the telephone companies would take a new look at the situation and would come to grips with this matter and do something about it. Of all the companies which provide services in this country I think the telephone companies have done the poorest job.
There is one other thing which provokes me a little, and I would hope the government would take a look at the telephone bills they receive for the long distance calls they place. I go to my telephone in my office in this building and make a long distance call to Guelph or Toronto. Thirty seconds later I pick up the receiver of my telephone and try to dial a local number. What do I get? I get long distance. If the call happens to extend more than three minutes I am charged an extra minute for those 30 seconds. Do the people of this country realize that most of us who place three-minute long distance telephone calls are being charged 30 per cent extra on such calls? This is the only business I know of that operates that way, and one can do nothing about it. Telephone companies to me are not well run businesses. I think it is time the telephone companies realized that their service is not quite as good as they like to think it is.

I would like to ask the minister if he would recommend to the board of transport commissioners that they take a look at the handling of communications in this country.
I know the same situation obtains in most of the provinces, but the Bell Telephone Company is particularly at fault. It is no doubt the largest telephone company, and it has set an extremely bad example. I would hope that the minister with his capacity for getting things done could suggest to the board of transport commissioners that the board has the means of telling the telephone companies to take a look at their service to see if they could improve it.
If this is done I am sure we will not have thousands of people being told they will get a telephone when one is available, which may be a year from the date on which they make application. That situation was understandable at the end of the war and it might have been tolerated five years after the end of the war, but to have this situation existing 11 or 12 years after the cessation of hostilities is completely unrealistic, and it is nonsense to suggest to people that they should wait for a year to have a telephone installed.

Mr. Chairman, it is with a great deal of regret that I break my self-imposed silence of nearly two weeks' duration to make a few remarks on the estimates of the Department of Transport, particularly as they affect the maritime ports and Saint John, which is my main consideration.
At first glance the estimates appear to indicate that the past year has been a good one. I think for the first time traffic and tonnage are up, construction has been moving along at Saint John and Halifax and the local spirit is picking up. However, the situation is not quite so good as far as longterm planning for the future of these ports is concerned. This is a worry to all of us in the east.
I shall begin by referring to the St. Lawrence seaway. The minister was in Saint John in February of this year and viewed the harbour there. We were very glad indeed to see him in the old loyalist city. While there the minister made a remark to the effect that he thought the St. Lawrence seaway would benefit the maritimes to some extent. I do not know what the result will be, and I do not think anyone is qualified to say. We were disappointed that the matter of the seaway had not been considered in relation to the ports there to the degree that the other economic effects of the seaway were considered.
Two or three things come to my mind with respect to the seaway and its impact on our

future development. I think first of the icebreaking activity that is carried on each year to an increasing extent in the St. Lawrence. There is an article of recent date which suggests that there is considerable merit in the year-round navigability of the St. Lawrence, but the suggestion is made that it would be necessary to spend large sums of money on improvements designed to conserve the warmth of lake Ontario. The second suggestion which concerns me is that a large number of small icebreakers could be maintained to keep the shipping channel open.
I notice in the estimates of the department this year that three new icebreakers are mentioned. I also notice that according to a recent report the Russians have now completed an atomic energy powered icebreaker which it is anticipated will overcome the icebreaking difficulties they have experienced. This is an atomic powered icebreaker especially designed to meet their problems, and probably before long we will have plans for a similar project in this country.
I would like to refer to another matter somewhat along the same line of the icebreaking activity that occurs in the St. Lawrence. I have spoken about this matter before, as have other hon. members who are perhaps more qualified to deal with it. We all remember that on April 23 of this year an accident occurred involving the grounding of a ship in the St. Lawrence. The minister was questioned about it in the house. A veteran Quebec city navigator, Mr. Roger Arcand, is reported to have said that the authorities were pushing traffic ahead too early, and this caused the situation that developed. The exact words of Mr. Arcand as reported in the Montreal Gazette of April 23, 1956, were:
Authorities are running great hazards in pushing shipping through too early.
We all know about the early season the St. Lawrence had. I have only one thing to say in this connection. In view of the good work that is being done in relation to short-term planning, and in view of the publicity the department is giving to the ports and the booklets it is publishing, the long-term view for the future is not being properly attended to. We must have a statement as to the future plans of the department with regard to safeguards, and icebreaking in particular. We want to know what is to be the future of our maritime ports if it is found possible to keep open the St. Lawrence throughout the year.
There is also a lack of long-term planning with respect to shipping through our maritime ports. The city of Saint John was the
67509-447i
Supply-Transport
site of a recent meeting of the Canadian port committee, at which time Mr. W. C. Perron of Ottawa made the statement that Canadian ports-I suggest that this is particularly true of the maritime ports-are in a serious position, and encouragement must be given either locally or by the federal government to developing plans for the fostering of our ports. I shall not read the quotation because I do not want to take up the time, but I mention it to indicate the serious problems which must be considered by the department in developing its future policy.
As I have said, we are pleased with the day to day plans in connection with construction and publicity for our ports, but the future of this investment by Canada is a matter of concern. We are wary and suspicious of the seaway. We wonder just how this icebreaking activity is going to be developed throughout the entire year. We notice a stepping-up of departmental plans in this regard. With modern inventions it may be possible to solve the problem of keeping the St. Lawrence open all year. We want to know where we fit into that picture. Even at this late hour I should like the minister to indicate what the experts of the department have to say in this regard.
Another matter that concerns our future is the lack of a definite policy with respect to our merchant fleet. We read recently that 24 nations are meeting in London to consider the Suez situation, and Canada is not to be one of them. It is all very well to sit back and say that here is some responsibility we will not have to accept or worry about, but we must not forget that those 24 nations have much more prestige in foreign affairs than we have simply because we do not have merchant ships which would be using the canal.
We all know what has been said in the past about our merchant fleet. I mention this again in the hope that the minister will take a look at the serious situation of our merchant fleet, and that attention will be given by the department on a long-term basis to dealing more seriously and generously with our maritime ports.

Mr. Chairman, my purpose in rising at this time to take part in this debate on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Transport is respectfully to draw the attention of the minister and his officials to several troublesome and acute problems connected with air and rail transportation which face the people in Alberta generally, and particularly those in the city of Edmonton. I am just as anxious as anyone else to expedite the business of this house. I shall therefore come to grips

Supply-Transport
with the problem quickly. In order that the minister may better appreciate the reasoning ot the people back home and their concern with respect to this matter, I should like to give a few facts as a background.
As the minister knows, it is my privilege to represent in this house one of the three Edmonton constituencies. That city continues to enjoy unprecedented development, and it is looked upon as one of the fastest-growing communities in Canada. We consider our development to be of national significance. The significance of our development is seen not only in the mounting population of that city. It is reflected in the volume of commerce as seen by the vast increase in passenger traffic and in wholesale and retail sales; and in all this the minister's department is concerned, as he knows very well, because it involves things brought into that area and affects every commodity that is transported through and sent out of that part of the country.
Like everything in Alberta, it is a story with drama. It is connected with the resourcefulness of our people and the thrill of developing the northwest. By reason of its geographic location I think Edmonton lends itself very well to being perhaps the most important shipping point for that north country and to winning for Canada an important place in intercontinental traffic. I have here a clipping from the Edmonton Journal for February 27, 1956, in which the following is stated:
Northern Mining and Edmonton
All signs point to a big season for mining and prospecting in the northland this summer . . .
From Edmonton's standpoint it is worth noting that a record-breaking season is expected in both the lake Athabasca and Great Slave lake mining fields. These are supplied from and through the city ...
All this activity in northern Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories, and to a lesser extent that in north-central British Columbia and the Yukon, is important to this "gateway" and supply centre. One feature which especially deserves the attention of Edmontonians is transportation. This is the key to northern mining development.
I do not care what variety of political opinions exist in this house; I think hon. members must agree that Edmonton is the logical air shipping centre for the great north land. However I would say that airport facilities there are totally inadequate. This has been recognized in the surveys being made by aviation authorities and international airlines systems which are pioneering in transcontinental passenger service such as Scandinavian Airlines, Canadian Pacific Airlines, Trans World Airlines and Northwest Airlines. The people back home in Edmonton believe that the federal

government is overlooking the tremendous advantages we have there, as is evidenced by the slow way in which they are proceeding with the building of the proposed international airport in that city.
I wish to make it quite clear, Mr. Chairman, that my remarks are not in any way to be construed as a criticism of the minister.
I will be the first to say that the minister is handling one of the heaviest of the departments and is doing the job admirably. However, I am expressing the views of the people back home, namely that until they see some enthusiasm and drive in connection with the project they will continue to believe that the authorities lack imagination and are bogged down with various political considerations. I just cannot understand why, in a jet age such as that in which we live, the government should continually lay plans that will bring benefits only 10 years or 20 years from today. In time of war we can proceed to get things done rapidly, but in time of peace we keep dragging our feet.
I just do not understand the reason for that difference in approach. After all the objectives are the same, namely to act quickly in the best interests of our people. There is no question at all that there have been unwarranted delays in the building of the international airport in the city of Edmonton. In looking back, one can see that it is a case of attrition that has been going on for many years.
I should just like to give the facts briefly, in rough chronological order, and these facts speak for themselves. About 1949 the city of Edmonton began to press the federal government for airport reallocation to the city of Edmonton. Some time later the federal government responded by promising to build one in the future. Five years later, namely in December, 1954, in a general statement issued by the minister and his colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, it was announced finally that Edmonton was to get a new major airport built to international standards, and that orders had been given for an examination of possible sites. Some seven months later, namely on June 16, 1955, in reply to my inquiry-as appears in Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, June 9, 1955- I was informed that no tenders had been called for and no survey contracts had been awarded. Approximately a year later the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys made a statement in Edmonton, and this is reported in the Edmonton Journal of April 5, 1956. The article is headed "Airport Survey to Begin Soon" and it reads in part as follows:
An aerial survey of the new federal airport near Nisku, 16 miles south of the city's centre on

the west side of the Calgary highway, will commence just as soon as the snow clears, Hon. George Prudham, Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, said Thursday.
The minister said initial contour work is necessary in the area which comprises 16 square miles. Surveys will be made of administration and other building sites and the locations of runways which will be two miles in length. Soil tests and other engineering work also has to be done.
"Before contracts can be awarded, all this engineering and other work has to be done. It will take most of the summer," said the minister. "The intention is to call for tenders next winter so that work can start just as early as possible in 1957," he added.
Mr. Chairman, I am not disputing the honesty of the minister's statement as to the date of the actual construction. However, I am saying that the time schedule is far too slow and that it ignores the urgencies of the matter. We grant that the present airport in Edmonton will serve us for some time, and in any event will be an addition to the proposed airport. However, for reasons of public safety, having regard to economic prospects, and in order to enable Edmonton to keep up with the quick pace of international air development, we ask the minister to reconsider the time schedule, and we urge that immediate action with the highest possible level of construction this summer be undertaken so as to achieve the early completion of this proposed international airport in Edmonton. Public opinion back home is fairly strong on this matter. I think the minister would like to know just how strong it is. In the Edmonton Journal of February 5, 1956, the following appears:
Faster Action on Airport Needed
Judging by mines minister Prudham's statement this week, the federal government has yet to recognize the need for moving along rapidly with the new Edmonton airport.
He says detailed surveying of the site is to commence in the spring and plans are to be ready for a call for tenders a year later. Construction presumably would be started sometime in 1957. This is not good enough. The citizens of Edmonton do not share the government's desire to stretch out the undertaking for political reasons. They want their city to be just as soon as possible in a position to take advantage of great new prospects in air transport.
It is astonishing and disturbing to look back and see how long the business of obtaining this necessity has taken to date.
It goes on to point out this:
Public patience has distinct limits, however, and no one should be more concerned about this fact of political life than the member from Edmonton who is a Liberal cabinet minister. He is in a position to get some action for his constituents and they will expect him to do so. Mr. Prudham should make it his aim to have construction commence this year. The future of his home city in intercontinental air transport, a matter which should be of more than passing interest to him, is waiting on his efforts.
Supply-Transport
The second problem, Mr. Chairman to which I wish to call attention is one of long standing, and it is becoming more burdensome and complex day by day. I refer to the ever increasing discriminatory freight rates imposed on the prairie provinces generally and the people of Alberta in particular. I wish to point out to the house that in the matter of freight rates we are the hardest hit province in Canada. It is clearly an injustice that should not be tolerated by the federal government. I wonder whether hon. members know that we in Alberta are called upon to pay rates from eastern Canada in many cases twice as great as the rates on the same goods from eastern Canada to Vancouver, even though the city of Vancouver is some 600 miles farther west than Edmonton. Does the government know that many industries and concerns interested and willing to come to our province for various purposes are unable to do so by reason of the vicious freight structure? I should like to know whether all the people of Canada know that the recent decision of the board of transport commissioners hoisting freight rates by 7 per cent was ordered before the evidence was allowed to be heard from the railways or the opponents of this increase.
In doing this I believe the commission acted without precedent, and in fact ignored the submission made by the eight provinces. As reported in the Star Phoenix of June 12, 1956, by John LeBlanc, Canadian Press staff writer:
Alberta counsel J. J. Frawley, speaking for the lawyers for eight governments present at the session said they do not believe the railways have made a case "for any increase, interim or otherwise".
There have been other statements made by people in that connection. Mr. Ben S. Plumer, chairman of the Alberta wheat pool, stated in Calgary that the railways did not have to prove their need for greater revenues, even though the federation of agriculture filed a vigorous protest. In handling the railway submission in this manner the board has set a dangerous precedent. Further, James Patterson, president of the Manitoba farmer's union, charged that the board had granted a freight rate increase to the railways before giving the effective groups a full opportunity to express their views on the matter. The producers' share of the consumer dollar has reached an all-time low, and the economy of farm production is completely lost in the rapidly climbing marketing and transportation costs. I think, Mr. Chairman, this type of action is setting back the relationship and the progress that we have made over the years.
There is another very serious problem, in addition to the pyramiding freight rates,

Supply-Transport
which is hitting hard at our western producers and consumers. That is, the present administration is allowing the technique of agreed charges to overcome the one and one-third rule established by parliament in 1951. At that time it was clearly shown that the one and one-third rule was in the public interest. May I point out that people everywhere are asking just what happened to the recommendations of the Turgeon commission report which resulted in 1951 in the enactment of reform legislation.
I think we will all recall that at that time the legislation enacted forbade the railway companies from imposing any rates to Alberta in excess of one and one-third times the same rates for commodities from the east to the west coast. During the past year we have had a rash of agreed charges covering just about every type of commodity from frozen food to canned goods, varnishes and so forth. Let me just give an example of how serious these freight rate agreed charges are. Steel bars shipped from Hamilton to Vancouver cost $1.30 per hundredweight. The same steel bars shipped from Hamilton to Edmonton cost $3.23 per hundredweight. Sheet steel shipped from Hamilton to Vancouver costs $1.10 per hundredweight. The same sheet steel shipped from Hamilton to Vancouver costs $2.30 per hundredweight. Paints and varnishes shipped from Montreal to Vancouver cost $2.25 per hundredweight. The same shipment of ingredients to Edmonton costs $3.35 per hundredweight.
Here is another example, and I quote this by reason of the tremendous amount of construction in the Edmonton area at this time. Glass windows shipped from Montreal to Vancouver cost $2.56 per hundredweight. Glass windows shipped from Montreal to Edmonton cost $3.32 per hundredweight. It seems to me that simply because people reside outside of a community in which there is cheap water competition, that is no reason for this government penalizing them by unfair freight rates. It is my view that if there are inadequacies in revenue to the railway companies, if and when they are properly justified these problems can best be resolved at the government level where the whole country shares the load and not as it now is, with the prairie provinces paying the full shot.
We all know the maritime provinces enjoy the benefit of government subsidies in freight rates. I believe they have had them since away back in 1927. In the matter of these discriminatory freight rates which we have to face I think the situation is very similar to the one that existed in the United States prior to 1918, when such discrimination was

imposed upon those states which lie directly south of the province of Alberta, such as New Mexico, Idaho, Nevada and so forth. In the early 1920's they enacted their interstate commerce act and got rid of that discrimination once and for all.
This points out clearly that in the matter of an equitable freight structure we Canadians are 40 years behind the times. We know that by reason of section 52 of the Railway Act the minister has the right to vary or rescind any of the decisions of the board of transport commissioners. I would suggest to him that he approach this serious problem with a view to a complete overhaul of the whole freight structure, because certainly the provinces in the west have been milked far too long and far too much.

Mr. Chairman, I could not let the discussion on this matter pass without asking the Minister of Transport to direct his attention to the problem of the maritime provinces. We in Nova Scotia are at the end of a long transport haul, and we are very remote from the central market. The Maritime Freight Rates Act was designed to even up this disparity, but with the succeeding increases in freight rates the advantage of the statute to Nova Scotia has been very greatly lessened.
I would respectfully ask the minister to give a searching reconsideration to the position of Nova Scotia in respect of these freight rates, with a view to restoring the traditional role of the maritime freight rates.
