Mr. Chairman, since I have had the honour of sitting in this house I have, on several occasions, voiced the grievances and complaints of the people of the kingdom of Saguenay and of Chicoutimi county in particular, regarding the quality of the transportation services given us by that public-owned company called the Canadian National Railways.
I must say frankly and quite humbly that, although my remarks have been judged quite to the point by my electors, they have not brought about the results I expected. There is a French saying to the effect that days follow days but that they are not all alike. Well that old saying certainly does not apply to us, as far as railroad service is concerned. Since 1887 or 1888, when the railroad was completed which has Chicoutimi as its terminus, the situation has changed very little or not at all.
While the jet planes of the R.C.A.F. station at Bagotville whizz by at supersonic speed, and while Chicoutimi motorists can get to Quebec city in two hours, our good old rail-

road still takes nine hours to cover the distance between the ancient capital and the metropolis of the Saguenay.
While in all other fields of economic activity, we are at the forefront, we lag way behind as far as railway passenger and freight service is concerned.
In the matter of speed and comfort, we are still in the horse and buggy days. If we want food on the train, we either have to bring a lunch, as the first settlers used to do, or be content with sandwiches which are sold at fancy prices. Even then, we cannot have those sandwiches toasted because the toaster only works if the train is travelling at full speed, which it never does.
If the train leaves Montreal at 7 o'clock at night, it does not get into Chicoutimi until the following morning at 7.30, when it is on time. In other words, it takes 12J hours to cover a distance of 300 miles, which averages less than 25 miles per hour. Very often, especially during the winter, it comes in late.
There is further evidence. I shall quote a few paragraphs of a letter sent to the board of transport commissioners as well as to the president of the C.N.R. by the local chamber of commerce of the Saguenay district.
Jonquiere, Que., January 18, 1956.
Board of Transport Commissioners,
Ottawa. Ont.
Copy to Mr. Gordon, President, National System, Montreal, and to Mr. Gauthier, Superintendent, National System, Quebec.
Gentlemen:
At the last meeting of the chambers of commerce of the Saguenay district, we were shown a report on the very bad service given to our population by the railway during the holiday season.
It has been shown that the passenger train which normally arrives at Chicoutimi at 7.30 a.m. has sometimes been as much as 10 hours late. For your information, we have all the hours of arrival between December 18 and December 29 last.
This year, the railway cannot blame these delays on cold weather or snow since we have had very fair weather . . .
For the local Chamber of Commerce of the district of Saguenay (Sgd.) Phillippe Tremblay, Secretary.
At this point I call to witness my good friend, the very distinguished Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) with whom I had the privilege to travel to Chicoutimi on the 1st of May last. We were on our way to a ceremony which was to start at 9 o'clock in the morning, and we pulled into Chicoutimi at 10.30.
I let it be distinctly understood that I am not attaching any blame to the railway per-
Supply-Transport
sonnel. Far from it, as I know from experience that they fulfil their duties perfectly. From the conductor to the baggage man, all are efficient, devoted and courteous.
The engineer and fireman work wonders to deliver us safe and sound at our destination. Unfortunately they cannot eliminate curves, nor rush along at a hundred miles an hour on this snaky, meandrous line.
I offer no criticism of the minister since I know that he is kindly disposed on our behalf. He proved it by authorizing the construction of the St. Felicien-Chibouga-mau line. But I do blame the C.N.R. management and the government, who never bothered to listen to our representations or requests, and who never have given our area the attention it deserves.
I have said, and I am repeating now, that we are unfairly treated by the federal government. The deficiencies from which we are suffering, notably in Chicoutimi-antiquated station, inadequate and incomplete harbour facilities, lack of proper accommodation for postal and other official services, level crossings-all these can be blamed on the lack of interest of the Ottawa government.
Yet, our section of the country is, in the whole of Canada, one of those which pay the most taxes. That should be taken into account.
Without delay, the Canadian National Railways should act on pigeon-holed improvement projects about which, every once in a while, the vice-president of the company gives us a talk in Chicoutimi.
I urge the minister to use his influence in our favour and to demand that we be given decent treatment. The future of our business community depends on it.
It is inconceivable that it should take twice as much time to go from Montreal to Chicoutimi by railway as it takes by automobile.
Secondly, may I voice my support of the request sent to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) by the Association of Shipowners of the St. Lawrence and the Port Alfred chamber of commerce concerning the installation of a radio-telephone station on the Saguenay river.
An improvement of this type would be a great help for navigation on this river, and would also be very valuable to all those using it.
I hope that this request will be considered justified and that action will be taken accordingly.

Supply-Transport
I would also like to draw the minister's attention to the necessity of building a civilian airport in our district.
The lack of such an airport is a serious gap, considering the development of civil aviation and the fact that the R.C.A.F. base station at Bagotville does not allow private aircraft to land there.
The hon. minister wrote me recently to tell me that he does not think the time has come to authorize such a project.
If I may renew that request, I would ask him to reconsider his decision in the light of the new arguments which have been submitted to him by different public bodies of the region.
I would like now to call the attention of this house to a fact which has made me particularly happy, and it is that the title page of the recently distributed Canadian National timetable is printed in both our official languages. It is the first time, to my knowledge, that such a move is made, and I am happy to congratulate those who sponsored it.
We would be happier still if the facade of the new hotel being put up in Montreal would also indicate the French character of our country. In the meantime, let us be thankful for what has been done, and let us work and hope for what remains to be done.
Trans-Canada Air Lines have also put out on June 1 last a French issue of their timetables. It likewise deserves congratulations, and the progress of bilingualism in the administration of crown corporations is noteworthy. In conclusion, I would ask the minister whether it would be possible for him to table in this house a copy of the contract between the Canadian National authorities and the U.S. controlled Hilton company, concerning the operation of the new hotel which is going up in Montreal.

Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will get his estimates under way and I do not want to hold them up unnecessarily. I am going to try to be the very soul of brevity and put before him the pith and substance of what is a very strong case for the western people, at least, in relation to what now seems to me to be an abomination.
First of all I would like to invite the minister to come up to my constituency this summer, if we ever get through here, and I would suggest that he come about blueberry time. I would like him to see for himself what is going to happen when the Pacific Great Eastern Railway has completed its line

into Dawson Creek on the south side of the Peace river and into Fort St. John on the north side. There will be a gap of something between 90 and 100 miles between Hines creek on the north side of the river and Fort St. John that will be left without a railway link, and consequently there will be no outlet to the Pacific coast for all the territory on the north side of the Peace river. Therefore it will be necessary for the people in the great northern Peace river country to pay for that very long back haul of 275 to 300 miles into the city of Edmonton before they can even start to get their goods out to markets either on the Pacific coast or at the head of the lakes.
There is no reason why the railways of Canada should not complete this link, and there is every good reason for doing so. I believe the people there have a good case, and it would be well for the minister to look into it by a personal visit to see for himself what is involved. I entreat the minister to come out to that part of the country and see this situation for himself as soon as he possibly can. That is all I am going to say about the matter. By the way, I might add that we will treat the minister very well if he comes out to see us and we will ensure that he gets plenty of blueberries. Incidentally, he may be able to gain a few votes, too, if he comes out to that territory; and I think that is a fair suggestion coming from me.
I would like to say a word about what has been in the past a very great interest of mine. I refer to the great increases in freight rates that have taken place since 1945. Freight rates in western Canada have increased by more than 100 per cent since that year. Those people who live on farms out there have to pay freight rates both ways, that is on everything they buy coming westward and everything they sell that goes eastward, and they are beginning to wonder what is the end of this thing and how in the world they can ever find justice.
A few years ago there was a concerted outcry by members of parliament from western Canada against what was then a very discriminatory set of freight rates. It was largely because the members of the various parties in this house forgot politics and united in that outcry that we were able to obtain the appointment of a royal commission that went into the whole matter, and after their studies were complete they recommended amendments to the Railway Act to provide for overcoming the discrimination through the use of the one and a third freight rate rule and the equalization principle.

I am now suggesting that the time has come when members of parliament from the western provinces should again forget their political affinities for the time being and unite in an outcry against the injustice which is prevailing today. I think this must be done, and I believe it is the only way we can strengthen the minister's hand in accomplishing this. I am not blaming the minister at all, nor am I blaming his department. I am saying, however, that the people of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have been euchred-and I used the term "euchred" advisedly-out of the benefit of the one and a third rule established by this parliament.
Those people thought they had something when the amendments to the Railway Act were made some years ago, and as a matter of fact they did have something; but the weapon the railways used to euchre the western people out of the benefits under the one and a third rule was agreed charges. These are contract charges; that is what they are. These charges are increasing by leaps and bounds. They are coming in great numbers every day. The railways are making increasing use of them as a means of circumventing the legislation passed by this parliament, and they are doing so deliberately. Agreed charges are not only increasing but the tragedy of the situation is that the board in its weakness when it was confronted by what was virtually a threat made by the railways, yielded to the railways' demand that the one and a third rule should not apply to agreed charges.
When I speak of the threat I should say this. The railways virtually threatened that if the board insisted on the one and a third rule applying to agreed charges they would not haul on transcontinental rates at all. Of course the board in its weakness yielded, and since then the railways have completely nullified the one and a third rule which was written into the act by this parliament a few years ago. As a result we in the prairie provinces are right back where we were during the period from 1914 to 1951. That is, we are again subject to a set of rules that are grossly discriminatory in every respect. My friend the hon. member for Edmonton East has given enough examples of this, and I do not need to take the time of the committee to repeat them. I would like to refer, however, to the example of skelp which is used in the manufacture of pipe. We are using a great deal of skelp in the western provinces today. The rates on this commodity into Alberta from eastern Canada are set at $2 per hundredweight, but under an agreed charge arrangement the railways are hauling exactly the same material from Hamilton into Port
Supply-Transport
Moody in British Columbia for 95 cents. It costs more than twice as much to send it from central Canada to Alberta as it does to send it from central Canada to tidewater in British Columbia, which is 750 miles further along.
That is the kind of thing against which our people have set themselves and against which we are setting ourselves. If the members from western Canada would unite in demanding justice we would get justice in connection with this matter. As I say, some effective alternative must be found to the present practice of granting permissive flat horizontal percentage increases, because it is unfair and unjust when applied to the already discriminating freight rates.
I think I shall just leave it at that.

Mr. Chairman, this is the fourth time the estimates of this department have been before this committee, and I think if I were the minister I would give up. I did not intend to say anything at this time, but if there is to be a general debate on freight rates I shall have to say something, as freight rates constitute the principal problem facing Nova Scotia.
In his presentation to the Gordon commission dealing with the future of Canada in the economic field the premier of Nova Scotia stated emphatically that one of the greatest detriments to that province in its development from an industrial standpoint, and with respect to industry already there, is the freight rate structure. He contended that that prevented the products of the province getting into the main markets of Canada. I do not intend to go into this in detail as we have heard it time and time again. We have been talking freight rates ever since I came into this house.
I want to say to the minister that freight rates are not an east, west or central problem; they are a national problem. You must take a square look at them from the national standpoint. Year after year in this house we support the wage demands being made upon the railways, particularly the Canadian National. Every time there is a wage increase on the Canadian National it must be added to the bill. They are not accumulating any surpluses to take care of these increases and there is only one way they can get the revenue to meet their commitments; that is in the form of freight rates, passenger rates and so forth which must be paid by the public. Year after year we hear the cry from the east and the west and the centre, but mostly from the east and west because the centre is not affected.
Twenty-five years ago Nova Scotia had an offset to these freight rates provided by the Maritime Freight Rates Act, but rates in

Supply-Transport
that area have increased 100 per cent since that act was established while the rates in central Canada, in Quebec and Ontario, have not moved at all. The rates were equal when the Maritime Freight Rates Act was first drafted, but with the increase in rates in that area and with the rates in central Canada remaining stationary, any advantage we may have had has been lost.
I think the time has come when instead of arguing for agreed charges, for equalization and all these things which are only palliatives, we should take a square look at the matter from the national standpoint. I submit that what is needed today is an overall transportation policy which would integrate rail, water, air and truck transportation under a competent body, with regulatory bodies to see that the transportation which was economical in a certain area should be used there. I think that is the only solution I would suggest.
We have been arguing the other matter; we have had complaints from the far east and from the west, and we are getting in an impossible position. We find it impossible to move our goods to the markets in the east and the west, and we find it impossible to bring the things we need from those markets. Despite all we have heard about agreed charges and other palliatives the condition is getting worse and worse.
I believe that the railways are fast approaching the position in this country where they will have to be considered as service organizations. We just cannot continue to go on as we have been year after year. The Canadian Pacific makes a little money, but not from its railway operations; it has other operations which are subsidizing the railway. To a very limited extent the Canadian National gets a little outside revenue. I have been on the railway committee for the last 16 or 17 years and every time we look at the accounts of the Canadian National we find a huge deficit which the government must fix up or a small surplus in one year with an anticipated deficit the next. Quite often we would have Mr. Gordon tell us that he expected a surplus of half a million the next year, but that on the other hand he expected an increase in costs because of wage increases and adjustments, with the result that there would be an anticipated deficit.
You cannot go on like that. An alternative must be found. The alternative is not to try to modify the rates to the west or to do something for the east or to try to go on as we are. I think we must recognize what I indicated a moment ago, that we are fast approaching the point when the railways will
[Mr. Gillis.l
have to be looked upon as service organizations. We have two transcontinental lines with not enough people to use them to the extent that would make them profitable. They are necessary to the development of the country, but you cannot go on piling these costs on the consuming public year after year. It is retarding development in different sections of the country.
As I said a moment ago, we must integrate all the transportation systems of this country under a proper board with the power to regulate. Until we do that I think we are just talking to ourselves.

Mr. Chairman, I have been listening to hon. members participate in this debate and I notice that most of their observations have been with reference to the effect of freight rate increases upon the prairie provinces. It has been intimated that Alberta is suffering the most from the increases which have taken place. That is also the picture as far as British Columbia is concerned. These constantly mounting freight rates are imposing an additional hardship upon the province of British Columbia as well.
I am thinking particularly of those who must bring feed grain from the prairie provinces. In our province, especially the area which I have the honour to represent, the economy lends itself to the production of poultry products, the raising of dairy cattle and so on. Many people are dependent upon feed grain brought from the prairie provinces. A year and a half ago the freight rate subsidy was reduced by almost 50 per cent. The result was that out of the $3 million which the federal government hoped to save, about $1 million came out of the pockets of the British Columbia consumers when at the same time they used less than 10 per cent of the freight assistance grant. I would suggest that it is very unfair. I know I am speaking of Something that comes under the Department of Agriculture but I just want to show the position in which our farmers find themselves now with the increased rates. I feel that insult is being added to injury, because these people are going to be put in the position where it will be almost impossible for them to carry out operations in this field.
So I would suggest that the minister take some kind of action and do what he can to impress upon the board of transport commissioners and those responsible for these decisions that something will have to be done or we shall find that the economy in the whole of these western provinces is upset. That is all I want to say in this connection. I want to say again that I cannot see why the board

of transport commissioners should authorize an interim increase without hearing the case. That thought has been presented on several occasions this afternoon.
I had intended to speak a little longer in this connection but I do not want to take the time of the house, except to say this. When this government are paying out millions of dollars for storage charges because they cannot find markets, then why in the world is it that these freight rates are increasing to the extent that the markets are being lost because of the high freight rates?
There is just one other matter, and it is in connection with the Fraser river, which is a navigable river. I should like to call the minister's attention to some facts I placed on the record earlier this session-I shall not take the time to repeat them-regarding the Fraser river and the necessity for some action to dredge and channel it in order to take care of many of the problems arising there. At the time of the building of the Agassiz bridge-
That is a matter of public works. Would the hon. member co-operate-
I think the Department of Transport has the responsibility for shipping and so on-
Not the dredging.

I am talking about shipping. At the time of the building of that bridge, if 1 understand the facts correctly, the provincial government was forced to change its plans, to make the span higher to facilitate the passage of shipping under that bridge. I think it cost them an additional $1 million or so to make that alteration. The whole area is becoming more and more industrialized. Industry is opening up and wants to open up, yet the river is not suitable for navigation because of the sandbars, the lack of channels and so on. I am just making this request, that the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Public Works get together and try to work out some solution to the problem, because in doing so they will not only take care of the problems in regard to transportation but also the problems of river erosion and so on. I just make the request that these departments co-operate in working out a solution to the problem.

I would, in the very few minutes that remain, like to touch on one or two points very hastily, as there will not be further opportunities of discussing them. With respect to the question of freight rates, I am sure the hon. gentlemen will realize that it would be most inappropriate for me at this time, while the whole subject of freight rates is before the board of transport commissioners, to say anything on this subject one way or the other; because I assume that if those who are not satisfied with whatever decision may be rendered by the board carry an appeal to the governor in council, it would be unseemly that I should have already committed myself to any position on this very important subject.
I should like hon. members to remember when considering the question of freight rates that the wage agreements, the changes in wage scales in the current year, have added or will add to the wage bill for the two railways in the current year approximately $35 million, and in the year 1957 approximately $80 million. So I think the hon. gentlemen should not overlook that very important fact when they come to consider the position of the railways.
Consider paying a subsidy instead of increasing the freight rates.

I listened patiently to the hon. gentleman for most of the day, and perhaps he might spare me the interruptions in the very few minutes that remain.
I should like to say with regard to the Newfoundland services of the Canadian National Railways that since confederation the C.N.R. has invested something over $50 million in improvements in the system down there and, simply because that investment has not produced all the improvements that were expected and anticipated, a group of senior officials of the railway are to go to Newfoundland to see what can be done in the way of bringing about further improvements and what can be done to meet the demands that are being made upon the railway. In that connection I should mention that there are two vessels provided for the coastal service, the William Carson and the Bonavista, which should be in service without too much further delay.
I should like to say, with regard to the questions raised by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, that we shall have an opportunity for discussing icebreaking operations in the St. Lawrence when we come to a further item in the budget, and I shall reserve my comments on that subject until that item is dealt with.

The same applies to the Edmonton airport, but I should like to tell the hon. member at once that when I went to Edmonton last year and saw the various sites being considered by the department for the new airport I said publicly at that time that nothing in the way of physical work could be done in this year, 1956, and that nothing could be done under intelligent, proper planning, until the beginning of 1957, when we hoped to be able to call tenders.
On the subjects of the one and one third rule and agreed charges, all I shall say is to suggest to hon. members who have spoken that they should read the last report of the royal commission presided over by Mr. Justice Turgeon, where the whole subject was discussed very fully and where the decision was reached that the one and one third rule did not apply to agreed charges.
I hope that the remaining 95 items of the Department of Transport budget will pass more rapidly than the first.
